sessions.title: The Kite in the Tree
paragraphs: Maya had a new purple kite. It had a long, curly tail with yellow bows. One windy morning, Maya and her father walked to the city park. "This is a perfect kite day," Father said. Maya started running across the grass. The kite lifted up, higher and higher.

But then the wind gave a sudden, giant push. The kite flew into a very tall maple tree. The string was tangled on a high branch. Maya pulled and pulled, but the kite would not budge. "Oh no," she said. "My kite is stuck!" She felt like crying.

First, Maya tried jumping for it. She jumped as high as she could. Her fingers did not even get close. Then her father tried reaching for it. He was tall, but the branch was too high for him too. The kite just rested in the tree.

So Maya sat down on the grass to think. She held the string and watched the leaves. The wind was blowing one direction. Then it was blowing the other direction. Maya had an idea. "The wind carried it up there," she said. "Maybe the wind can carry it down."

Maya stood up and waited. When the wind was blowing away from the tree, she gave the string a gentle tug. It was not a hard pull. It was a tiny, careful tug. The kite wiggled. She tugged again. The string slipped off the branch!

Finally, the kite was free. It was dancing up into the sky. Maya cheered, and her father clapped. In the end, Maya learned something important. A hard pull is not always the answer. Sometimes you need to stop, notice, and think.

stops.question: What is the problem in this story? How did the story change in this part?
stops.lookFor: The kite got stuck in the tree; the story went from happy flying to a problem Maya has to fix.

stops.question: Why do you think the author shows Maya and her father trying things that do not work?
stops.lookFor: It shows the problem is hard and builds up to the real solution; the tries are events caused by the problem.

stops.question: How does Maya's idea from watching the wind connect to what she does now?
stops.lookFor: She noticed the wind changes direction, so she waits for it to blow away from the tree before she tugs.

questions.q: What is the problem, and what is the solution?
questions.a: The kite gets stuck in a tree. Maya waits for the wind to blow the other way and tugs softly until it slides free.

questions.q: Which signal words help you see the order of events?
questions.a: One windy morning, but then, first, then, so, finally, in the end.

questions.q: What changed for Maya from the middle of the story to the end?
questions.a: She went from upset and pulling hard to calm and thinking, and that helped her solve the problem.

sessions.title: Biscuit Will Not Come In
paragraphs: Eli had a little brown puppy named Biscuit. Biscuit loved the back yard. He liked sniffing the flowers and digging in the dirt. One morning the sky turned dark and gray. Mom said, "Rain is coming soon. Please bring Biscuit in."

But Biscuit did not want to come in. He was having too much fun. Eli stood by the open door and called, "Biscuit, come here!" Biscuit wagged his tail. Then he raced the other way. A raindrop landed on Eli's nose.

First, Eli started chasing Biscuit. Biscuit thought it was a game. He ran in a big circle. Eli ran in a big circle too. Around and around they went. Eli got tired, but Biscuit was not. He just kept going.

Then Eli opened the doggy treat box. He held out a biscuit and said, "Look, Biscuit!" Biscuit did not even look up. He was busy digging a hole by the fence. His nose was full of dirt. More rain was falling on the yard.

So Eli tried one new thing. He sat down on the step and got very quiet. He was not running. He was not yelling. He held out his hand and said, "Biscuit," in a soft voice. Biscuit stopped digging. He tilted his head. Then he trotted over and climbed into Eli's lap.
Finally, Eli took him in. The rain was pouring down. Eli dried Biscuit's muddy paws with a towel. In the end, Eli learned a good thing. A soft, calm voice can work better than a chase.

stops.question: What problem starts here? What caused it?
stops.lookFor: Biscuit will not come in before the rain; he is having too much fun in the yard.

stops.question: Why didn't chasing work? What did Eli's running make Biscuit think?
stops.lookFor: Biscuit thought the chase was a game, so running made the problem worse.

stops.question: The author keeps telling us about the rain. Why does the author add that detail each time?
stops.lookFor: The rain is getting worse, so it shows Eli is running out of time and the problem is getting bigger.

questions.q: What are the three things Eli tried?
questions.a: He chased Biscuit, offered a treat, and then sat still and called softly.

questions.q: Which try solved the problem, and why did it work?
questions.a: Sitting still and calling softly worked because it was calm and not a game, so Biscuit came to him.

questions.q: What is the setting, and why does it matter to the problem?
questions.a: The back yard as a storm comes in; the rain is why Biscuit has to come inside.

sessions.title: No Eggs Today
paragraphs: Nia loved baking with her grandpa. They had a big job today. Nia's class was having a party. She had promised to bring cookies. Grandpa got out the mixing bowl and the flour. Nia got out the sugar and butter. They put on their aprons.

But when Nia opened the fridge, she noticed a problem. The egg carton was empty. There were no eggs at all! "We need an egg for these cookies," Grandpa said. Nia looked at the kitchen clock. The party was the next day.

First, Nia searched the back of the fridge. She moved the milk and the jelly. She found a lemon and some cheese. She did not find an egg. Then she hurried next door to ask their neighbor. She rang the doorbell, but nobody was home.

Nia came back and sat at the table. She was feeling sad. "Now we can't bake," she said. Grandpa sat down beside her. He rested his chin in his hand to think. Then he looked at the fruit basket on the counter.

"I have an idea," Grandpa said. He picked up a yellow banana. "A mashed banana can hold cookie dough together, just like an egg." So Nia peeled the banana. She mashed it with a fork. They mixed it into the dough.

Finally, the cookies came out of the oven. They were soft and sweet, and they smelled like banana. Nia carried them to school in a metal tin. In the end, her class loved them. Nia said, "These are the best cookies ever."

stops.question: Why does the author tell us about the class party at the start?
stops.lookFor: It shows why the cookies matter and sets up the problem; Nia promised cookies, so she needs to bake.

stops.question: What caused Nia to look in the fridge and go next door?
stops.lookFor: There were no eggs, and she needed one for the cookies, so she tried to find one.

stops.question: How did Nia's feelings change in this part? Why?
stops.lookFor: She went from hopeful to sad because both tries failed and she thought they could not bake.

questions.q: What is the problem in this story?
questions.a: There are no eggs, and Nia needs to bake cookies for her class party.

questions.q: How did the problem get solved?
questions.a: Grandpa had the idea to use a mashed banana in place of the egg.

questions.q: Why do you think the author shows Nia trying things that do not work first?
questions.a: It shows the problem is hard and makes the solution feel more important at the end.

sessions.title: Kai in the Goal
paragraphs: Kai played on a soccer team called the Green Hawks. He loved running and kicking the ball. One afternoon his coach asked him to play goalie. The goalie has to stop the ball from going into the net. Kai agreed, but his stomach felt nervous.

The problem was that Kai was afraid of the ball. Whenever it came flying toward him, he turned his head away. He even closed his eyes. At practice, the ball landed in the net again and again. Kai felt terrible about letting his team down.

First, Kai asked his older sister for help at home. She kicked soft balls at him in the yard. But Kai still closed his eyes every time. Then he tried standing way back in the net. That did not help either, because the ball got past him even faster.

So Kai went to talk to Coach Rosa after practice. "I keep closing my eyes," he said. Coach smiled. "Lots of goalies feel that way at first," she said. "Try this idea. Watch the ball like it is your best buddy. Keep your eyes open the whole time."

Kai practiced every day that week. He repeated to himself, "Watch your buddy." Each day he kept his eyes open a little longer. Soon he could see the ball coming. His hands knew where to go. He started to stop more and more shots.

Finally, it was the day of the big game. A player on the other team kicked a powerful shot. Kai kept his eyes on the ball. He jumped and caught it! His team cheered. In the end, Kai was proud. He was not afraid of the ball anymore.

stops.question: What is Kai's problem? How is it different from what he expected in the first part?
stops.lookFor: He is scared of the ball and closes his eyes; at first he was excited to play, but now it is hard.

stops.question: Why do you think the author shows two tries that did not work?
stops.lookFor: To show the problem is hard to fix and to build up to the coach's advice.

stops.question: How does Coach Rosa's advice connect to what Kai does this week?
stops.lookFor: He uses her words, watch the ball like a buddy, and practices them every day until it works.

questions.q: What are the main events Kai goes through to solve his problem?
questions.a: He practices with his sister, stands farther back, asks Coach Rosa for help, and then practices her tip all week.

questions.q: What is the solution to Kai's problem?
questions.a: He learns to keep his eyes on the ball, and he makes a big save in the game.

questions.q: How did Kai change from the start to the end?
questions.a: He went from scared and closing his eyes to brave and proud.

sessions.title: Amara's Bean Plant
paragraphs: Amara's class had a garden in front of the school. Each kid got to plant one seed. Amara picked a green bean seed. She pushed it into the soft dirt and gave it a drink. Every morning, she ran out to check on it before the bell rang.

Soon a tiny green sprout came up. Amara was so happy. The plant grew taller each day. But one day she saw a problem. The plant was lying flat on the dirt. Its long stem had flopped over. Bugs could get to it, and the leaves were turning brown.

First, Amara thought the plant needed more water. She filled her cup to the top and poured it on. But the next day, the plant was still lying down. The dirt was just wet and muddy. Then she tried to stand it up with her hands. As soon as she let go, it fell over again.

So Amara went to ask her teacher, Miss Brooks. She came out to look. "Ah," she said. "Some bean plants are climbers. They grow long and thin, and they need something to hold on to. In nature they might wrap around another plant."

Miss Brooks gave Amara a tall wooden stick. She pushed it into the ground next to her plant. Then she tied the stem to the stick with a soft piece of string. She tied it gently so it would not hurt the stem.

Finally, the plant stood up tall. In a few days, it began to curl around the stick all by itself. It grew past Amara's knee and then past her waist. In the end, it even grew beans. Amara shared them with the whole class.

stops.question: The story says, but one day she saw a problem. How does the story change here?
stops.lookFor: It goes from the plant growing well to a problem: the plant has flopped over and could get hurt.

stops.question: Why didn't more water fix the problem? What does that tell you?
stops.lookFor: Water was not what the plant needed; Amara was guessing at the cause, so she needed to learn more.

stops.question: How does what Miss Brooks says connect to the problem?
stops.lookFor: She explains the cause: bean plants are climbers that need something to hold, which is why it fell over.

questions.q: What is the problem and what caused it?
questions.a: The bean plant fell over because it is a climber and had nothing to hold on to.

questions.q: What two things did Amara try before the solution?
questions.a: She gave it more water, and she tried to stand it up with her hands.

questions.q: What is the solution, and how do you know it worked?
questions.a: She tied the plant to a stick; it stood up, curled around the stick, and grew beans.

sessions.title: Theo's Loud Drum
paragraphs: Theo got a drum for his birthday. It was shiny and silver, and it came with two wooden sticks. Theo loved banging out a beat. Boom, tap, boom, tap! He wanted to practice all day long. He dreamed of starting a band someday.

But Theo had a baby sister named Hana. She took a long nap every afternoon. That was exactly when Theo came home from school. One afternoon he played his drum, and Hana woke up crying. Mom hurried in, looking tired. "Theo, the drum is too loud right now," she said.

First, Theo tried playing very softly. He tapped the drum with only the tips of the sticks. But it did not sound like music. It sounded like rain on a roof. It was not exciting at all. Then he put a pillow on top of the drum. Now he could only hear a dull thud.

So Theo sat down with Mom to talk about the problem. "I want to play my drum," he said. "And I want Hana to sleep." Mom thought for a minute. "Maybe we need a family plan," she said. "What if you practice when Hana is awake?"

They made a schedule together and hung it on the refrigerator. Theo would read and do his homework while Hana napped. When she woke up, it would be drum time. Theo drew a little drum on the schedule for every day.

Finally, the plan worked. Hana got her quiet nap. Later, Theo could play as loudly as he wanted. And guess what? Hana loved clapping along to the music. In the end, Theo had his first fan, and his first band had two members.

stops.question: What is the problem? Why does the author tell us about Hana's nap?
stops.lookFor: The drum is too loud while Hana naps; the nap detail is the cause of the problem.

stops.question: Why do you think the author shows the pillow and the soft tapping?
stops.lookFor: They are tries that did not work, so we see the problem is not easy to solve.

stops.question: How is Theo's new try different from his first two tries?
stops.lookFor: He talks with Mom and they make a plan together, instead of changing how he plays.

questions.q: What is Theo's problem?
questions.a: He wants to play his drum, but it wakes up his baby sister during her nap.

questions.q: What is the solution?
questions.a: They make a schedule so Theo plays when Hana is awake and does homework while she naps.

questions.q: How does the ending connect back to the beginning?
questions.a: Theo dreamed of a band at the start, and at the end Hana claps along like his first fan and band member.

sessions.title: Zoe and the Cloudy Sky
paragraphs: Zoe received a telescope from her grandpa. It was long and black, and it stood on three metal legs. Grandpa told her that if she looked at the moon through it, she would see craters. Craters are big round holes made when space rocks crash into the moon long ago.

That night, Zoe carried the telescope out to the back porch. She was so excited that she could hardly hold still. But when she looked up, the sky was full of thick gray clouds. She could not see the moon at all. She could not even see one star.

First, Zoe decided to be patient. She sat on the porch steps with a blanket around her shoulders. She waited and waited, but the clouds did not move. Then she tried looking through the telescope anyway. All she saw was a dark, fuzzy blur, so she went inside feeling disappointed.

The next night, Zoe ran outside again. Clouds covered the sky one more time. This time she called Grandpa. "The clouds keep hiding the moon," she said. Grandpa laughed kindly. "Space has been there a long time," he said. "It will still be there tomorrow. Let's check the weather together and make a plan."

So Zoe and Grandpa studied the weather report together. It said the sky would be clear on Friday evening. Zoe wrote it on the calendar. While she waited, she read a library book about the moon so she would know what to look for.

Finally, Friday came. The sky was clear and full of stars. Zoe pointed the telescope at the bright moon. She saw gray plains and dozens of round craters! In the end, Zoe learned that sometimes the best thing to do is plan and be patient.

stops.question: Why does the author explain what craters are at the very start?
stops.lookFor: So we know what Zoe hopes to see; it sets up what she wants before the problem happens.

stops.question: What caused Zoe to go inside feeling disappointed?
stops.lookFor: The clouds did not move, so she could not see anything, and her tries did not work.

stops.question: How is calling Grandpa different from what Zoe tried before?
stops.lookFor: She asks for help and they make a plan, instead of just waiting or trying anyway.

questions.q: What is the problem in the story?
questions.a: Clouds keep covering the sky, so Zoe cannot see the moon through her telescope.

questions.q: Name the events that happen because of the problem.
questions.a: She waits on the porch, looks through the clouds anyway, tries again the next night, and calls Grandpa.

questions.q: How is the problem solved?
questions.a: Zoe and Grandpa check the weather, plan for a clear night, and she sees the craters on Friday.

sessions.title: Omar and the Shy Crabs
paragraphs: Omar and his mom went to the beach on a warm, sunny morning. The tide was low, so small pools of water were left between the rocks. Mom said these were called tide pools. Tiny sea animals live in them. Omar wanted to see a crab more than anything.

Omar spotted a little green crab on a rock. He ran over fast to get a closer look. But the crab scuttled sideways and hid under the rock. Omar frowned. Every time he found a crab, it vanished before he could really see it.

First, Omar tried to sneak up on one. He tiptoed across the wet rocks, but his feet made little splashes. The crab hid again. Then he tried lifting a small rock to peek under it. Mom gently reminded him to put it back just the way he found it, so the animals would stay safe.

So Omar sat down on a dry rock to think. He watched the water. A tiny fish swam by. A snail moved slowly along the side of the pool. Omar noticed that the animals came out when everything was calm and quiet. Maybe the crabs were scared of him, not hiding from him on purpose.

Omar decided to try a new plan. He stayed very still on his rock and kept his hands in his lap. He did not talk or splash. He just watched the edge of the pool. Minutes went by. Then a little claw poked out from under a rock.

Finally, the green crab came all the way out. It walked sideways across the sand and waved its claws. Omar could see its tiny eyes and its striped legs. In the end, Omar smiled. He learned that being calm and patient helped him see much more.

stops.question: What problem does Omar have? What caused the crab to hide?
stops.lookFor: Every crab hides before he can see it; Omar ran over fast and scared it.

stops.question: Why do you think the author included Mom's reminder to put the rock back?
stops.lookFor: It shows how to treat tide pool animals with care, and it shows that lifting rocks is not a good way to solve the problem.

stops.question: How does what Omar notices here connect to his next plan?
stops.lookFor: He sees that animals come out when it is calm, so he decides to sit still and quiet.

questions.q: What is the setting, and why does it matter?
questions.a: Tide pools at the beach at low tide; that is where the crabs live and hide.

questions.q: What did Omar try that did not work?
questions.a: Running over, sneaking on tiptoe, and lifting a rock to peek.

questions.q: What is the solution, and what did Omar learn?
questions.a: He sat still and quiet until a crab came out; he learned that calm and patience help.

sessions.title: Lila's Stegosaurus
paragraphs: Lila's class was learning about dinosaurs. Each student had to make a model of one dinosaur for the science fair. Lila picked the stegosaurus. It had big, flat plates standing up along its back and sharp spikes on its tail. She thought it was the coolest dinosaur of all.

Lila made the body out of green clay. Then she shaped ten flat plates and pressed them onto the back. But when she stood the model up, the plates slid off and fell onto the table. She tried again. Plop, plop, plop! They fell off every time.

First, Lila used more clay to stick the plates on. That just made them heavier, so they fell even faster. Then she wrapped tape around the plates. The tape held them, but it looked silly and shiny. It did not look like a real dinosaur at all. Lila felt like giving up.

So Lila asked her dad for help. He picked up one of the plates and turned it in his hand. "Buildings have strong beams hidden inside them," he said. "Maybe your plates need something strong inside them too." Lila thought about that. She looked around the kitchen for ideas.

Lila found a box of toothpicks. She pushed half of a toothpick into the bottom of each plate. Then she pushed the other half into the dinosaur's back. The toothpicks were hidden inside the clay, just like the beams in a building.

Finally, all ten plates stood up straight and tall. Lila added spikes to the tail the same way. In the end, her stegosaurus looked great at the science fair. Lila told everyone how she had solved the falling plate problem.

stops.question: Why do you think the author describes the stegosaurus plates at the start?
stops.lookFor: The plates become the problem later, so the author shows them first to set up the story.

stops.question: What caused Lila to feel like giving up?
stops.lookFor: Her tries did not work: more clay made the plates fall faster and tape looked silly.

stops.question: How does Dad's idea about buildings connect to what Lila does here?
stops.lookFor: She uses toothpicks hidden inside the clay like beams inside a building.

questions.q: What is Lila's problem?
questions.a: The clay plates keep falling off her stegosaurus model.

questions.q: Why didn't more clay solve the problem?
questions.a: More clay made the plates heavier, so they fell off even faster.

questions.q: What is the solution, and who helped her think of it?
questions.a: Toothpicks inside the plates hold them up; Dad's idea about hidden beams helped her.

sessions.title: The Cardboard Castle
paragraphs: Jordan and his cousin Ava had a huge pile of empty cardboard boxes in the garage. "Let's build a castle big enough to sit inside," Jordan said. Ava grabbed the tape, and they got to work right away. They planned tall walls, a door, and even a tower.

They stood four big boxes up in a square and taped the corners together. It looked great for about one minute. But then one wall leaned in, and the whole castle folded down flat. Jordan sighed. Every time they built the walls up high, the castle fell over.

First, they used more tape. They wrapped it around the corners again and again until the roll was almost gone. The walls still wobbled and bent. Then they tried making the walls taller so they would look stronger. That only made things worse, because the tall walls fell down even faster.

So Jordan and Ava took a break and looked at a picture book about real castles. Ava noticed something. Many old walls had thick stone pieces sticking out from the sides. "Those are like arms holding the wall up," she said. Jordan pointed to a bridge in another picture. It had metal pieces shaped like triangles.

The cousins had an idea. They cut cardboard triangles and taped one to the inside of each corner. The triangles pushed against the walls and kept them from bending. Next, they added a cardboard roof across the top to hold the square together.

Finally, the castle stood tall and steady. Jordan and Ava crawled inside with flashlights and a bag of snacks. Nothing wobbled at all. In the end, they learned that being strong is not just about using more stuff. It is about building with the right shape.

stops.question: What changed in this paragraph? What problem do the cousins have now?
stops.lookFor: The castle went from looking great to falling flat; the walls keep falling when built high.

stops.question: Why did the taller walls make the problem worse? What does that show about their tries?
stops.lookFor: Taller walls were heavier and wobbled more; it shows they had not found the real cause yet.

stops.question: Why do you think the author has the cousins look at a book here?
stops.lookFor: It is how they find the idea for the solution; the pictures connect to the triangles they use next.

questions.q: What is the problem in this story?
questions.a: The cardboard castle keeps falling over when the walls are built up high.

questions.q: What did the cousins learn from the book that helped solve the problem?
questions.a: Real walls and bridges use supports and triangle shapes to stay strong.

questions.q: How does the lesson at the end connect to the tries that did not work?
questions.a: More tape and taller walls failed because using more stuff was not the answer; the right shape was.

sessions.title: The Gate on Level Nine
paragraphs: Ben and his little sister Sofia loved playing a video game about a floating island. In the game, you explored caves, picked up shiny gems, and solved puzzles to open new places. One rainy Saturday, they reached Level Nine. A giant stone gate blocked the path, and they could not get past it.

There was a big red button on the ground near the gate. When Ben's character stepped on it, the gate slowly opened. But as soon as he stepped off to run through, the gate slammed shut again. Ben tried over and over, and he got more upset each time.

First, Ben tried to run faster. He pressed the buttons as fast as he could, but the gate always closed before he reached it. Then he looked for a secret path around the gate. He found only rocks and trees. At last, he tossed the controller onto the couch.

"I quit," Ben said. Sofia picked up the other controller. "Can I try?" she asked. Ben almost said no, because he thought she was too little for such a hard part of the game. Then he noticed something on the screen. There was room for two characters, and the game had a two-player mode.

So Ben and Sofia played the level together. Sofia's character stood on the red button and held the gate open. Ben's character ran straight through. On the other side, he found a second button that kept the gate open for Sofia to follow.

Finally, both characters made it past the gate, and a shower of gems fell from the sky. Sofia cheered and gave her brother a high five. In the end, Ben realized the puzzle was never meant for one player. It was a teamwork puzzle all along.

stops.question: What is the problem? What causes the gate to close?
stops.lookFor: Ben cannot get through the gate; it shuts as soon as he steps off the button.

stops.question: How do Ben's feelings change across his tries? Why does the author show that?
stops.lookFor: He gets more frustrated until he quits; it builds up the problem before the turning point.

stops.question: Why is it important that Ben notices the two-player mode right here?
stops.lookFor: It is the turning point; it connects Sofia's offer to the solution.

questions.q: What are the events Ben tries before the solution?
questions.a: He tries to run faster, looks for a secret path, and then quits.

questions.q: What is the solution to the problem?
questions.a: Ben and Sofia play together: one holds the button while the other runs through.

questions.q: How did Ben's thinking about Sofia change from the middle to the end?
questions.a: He thought she was too little to help, but in the end she was the key to solving the puzzle.

sessions.title: A Card for Miss Grant
paragraphs: Every afternoon, a mail carrier named Miss Grant walked down Rosa's street with a heavy bag of mail, and she waved at every kid she saw, even on hot days and cold, rainy days. One day, Rosa decided that she wanted to thank Miss Grant for all of her hard work.

Rosa made a card with markers and glitter. On the front, she drew Miss Grant smiling beside her mail bag. Inside, she wrote, "Thank you for bringing our mail." But there was a problem. Rosa got home from school after the mail came, so she never saw Miss Grant anymore.

First, Rosa waited by the front window on a day off from school. After an hour, she left to get a snack, and when she came back, the mail was already in the box. Then she asked her neighbor to hand Miss Grant the card. But the neighbor was going away for a week.

So Rosa asked her dad for advice. "Miss Grant opens our mailbox every single day," he said. "What is one place she will always look?" Rosa's eyes lit up, because she suddenly knew exactly where to put her card. She just needed Miss Grant to know it was for her.

Rosa wrote "For Miss Grant, our mail carrier" on a big envelope in bright letters. She put the card inside and placed it in the mailbox. Then she lifted the little red flag on the side. That flag tells the mail carrier that something is waiting.

The next afternoon, Rosa hurried to the mailbox after school. Her card was gone, and in its place was a small note. It said, "Thank you, Rosa. You made my whole day!" In the end, Rosa smiled, because she had finally found a way to say thank you.

stops.question: Why does the author tell us that Miss Grant works on hot days and rainy days?
stops.lookFor: It shows why Rosa wants to thank her; it gives the reason for the whole story.

stops.question: What caused each of Rosa's tries to fail?
stops.lookFor: She left the window to get a snack and missed Miss Grant, and the neighbor was going away.

stops.question: How does Dad's question help Rosa think in a new way?
stops.lookFor: It makes her think about where Miss Grant always goes, so she thinks of the mailbox.

questions.q: What does Rosa want, and what is the problem?
questions.a: She wants to give Miss Grant a thank-you card, but she is never home when the mail comes.

questions.q: What is the solution?
questions.a: She leaves the card in the mailbox in a labeled envelope and raises the flag.

questions.q: How does the ending show the problem was solved?
questions.a: The card is gone, and Miss Grant left a note thanking Rosa.

sessions.title: The Birthday Breakfast
paragraphs: Malik had a big plan for his mom's birthday on Saturday. He wanted to surprise her with pancakes and berries in bed. He had practiced making pancakes with his dad for weeks, so he felt ready. There was just one tricky part to his plan.

His mom was always the first person awake in the whole house. She got up before the sun every morning to go for a walk. By the time Malik opened his eyes, she was usually sipping tea in the kitchen. How could he surprise her if she was already up?

First, Malik set his alarm clock for very early one morning, just to practice. But he was so sleepy that he turned it off and rolled over, and when he woke up, Mom was already back from her walk. Then he tried staying up all night, but he fell asleep on the couch before ten.

Worried that his plan would fail, Malik whispered the whole problem to his dad. Dad grinned and thought for a while. "What if we ask Mom to sleep in as her first present?" he said. "I will help her rest, and you can wake me when you are ready to cook."

On Friday night, Dad told Mom that her only job on her birthday morning was to relax. He set out her favorite book and an extra pillow. Malik set his alarm for seven o'clock and put it across the room, so he would have to get up to turn it off.

Finally, the alarm rang, and Malik jumped out of bed. He and Dad made a tall stack of pancakes and carried the tray upstairs, where Mom was still snuggled under the blanket. In the end, her happy smile was the best present Malik could have asked for.

stops.question: Why does the author tell us Malik practiced pancakes with his dad?
stops.lookFor: It shows he is ready to cook, so the real problem is something else: the surprise.

stops.question: How does this paragraph explain the tricky part of the plan?
stops.lookFor: It gives the cause of the problem: Mom wakes up first, so she could ruin the surprise.

stops.question: How is Malik's choice in this paragraph different from his first two tries?
stops.lookFor: He asks for help instead of trying to change his own sleep, and Dad has a new idea.

questions.q: What is the problem in the story?
questions.a: Mom always wakes up first, so it is hard to surprise her with breakfast in bed.

questions.q: What did Malik try that did not work, and why?
questions.a: He set an early alarm but turned it off, and he tried staying up late but fell asleep.

questions.q: How was the problem solved?
questions.a: Dad asked Mom to sleep in, and Malik put his alarm across the room so he had to get up.

sessions.title: Bubbles and Brave Faces
paragraphs: Imani started swimming lessons at the community pool in the summer. She loved splashing in the shallow end. Her teacher, Coach Kim, was patient and funny. By the third week, every kid in her group was learning to swim with their faces in the water.

The problem was that Imani did not like water on her face. Whenever she tried putting her face in, she popped right back up, coughing and wiping her eyes. She started to feel left behind as her friends glided past.

First, Imani decided to just push through it. She took a huge breath and shoved her face in fast, but water went up her nose. Then she tried wearing her goggles extra tight. Her eyes stayed dry, but she still felt nervous and came up after one second.

After class, Coach Kim sat with Imani on the edge of the pool. "Let's try something slower," he said. "Instead of holding your breath, hum and blow bubbles out of your nose. The bubbles keep the water out." He showed her how to start with her chin, then her mouth, and then her whole face.

So every day that week, Imani practiced blowing bubbles in the bathtub at home. She started with her chin and slowly worked her way up, counting how long she could last. On Monday it was three seconds, but by Friday she could blow bubbles for ten seconds without feeling scared.

Finally, at her next lesson, Imani put her face in the water and hummed. She kicked her legs and reached her arms forward. When she looked up, she had swum all the way across the pool! In the end, Imani learned that going slowly can be the bravest way to go.

stops.question: What is Imani's problem, and how is it making her feel?
stops.lookFor: She does not like water on her face, so she cannot swim like her group, and she feels left behind.

stops.question: Why do you think the author shows Imani rushing first?
stops.lookFor: It shows a try that did not work, and it sets up the opposite idea of going slowly.

stops.question: How does Coach Kim's advice connect to what Imani does at home?
stops.lookFor: She practices the bubble steps he taught her, starting with her chin, and counts to see her progress.

questions.q: What are the main events that happen because of Imani's problem?
questions.a: She rushes and gets water up her nose, tries tight goggles, gets advice from Coach Kim, and practices at home.

questions.q: What is the solution?
questions.a: Blowing bubbles out of her nose and going step by step lets her swim with her face in the water.

questions.q: How does the lesson at the end connect to her first try?
questions.a: Her first try was rushing, which failed; the lesson is that going slowly worked better.

sessions.title: Leo's Plant Helper
paragraphs: Leo grew tomato plants in big pots on his back porch. He watered them every evening, and small green tomatoes were starting to grow. One night at dinner, his parents announced that the family would visit Grandma for a long weekend. Leo was thrilled, but then he thought about his plants.

It was the middle of summer, and the days were hot and dry. Tomato plants need water often, especially in the heat. Without water for four days, the leaves would droop, and the tomatoes might never turn red. Leo did not want his hard work to be wasted.

First, Leo asked his neighbor if she could water the plants. But she was going away that same weekend. Then he tried setting a pot inside a big bowl of water. The next morning, he discovered that a squirrel had tipped the bowl over and splashed water all over the porch.

So Leo decided to invent something. He needed a way to give the plants water slowly, so it would last for days. He thought about how a dripping faucet keeps going for a long time. Then his mom handed him some empty plastic bottles from the recycling bin.

With his mom's help, Leo poked a few tiny holes in each bottle cap. He filled the bottles with water and screwed the caps on tight. Then he turned each bottle upside down and pushed the top deep into the soil, where water began to drip out one drop at a time.

Finally, the family left for Grandma's house. When they came home four days later, he ran straight to the porch. The soil was still damp, and the plants were standing tall. In the end, Leo's bottle drippers had saved his tomatoes.

stops.question: How does the family's news cause the problem in this story?
stops.lookFor: Being away for the weekend means nobody will water the plants.

stops.question: Why do you think the author explains what tomato plants need here?
stops.lookFor: It shows why the problem is serious and why Leo cannot just skip watering.

stops.question: How does the idea of a dripping faucet connect to the problem?
stops.lookFor: Leo needs water to come out slowly over days, and a drip keeps going a long time.

questions.q: What is Leo's problem?
questions.a: His family is going away for four hot days, and nobody can water his tomato plants.

questions.q: Why didn't the bowl of water work?
questions.a: A squirrel tipped it over, so the water spilled.

questions.q: What is the solution, and how do you know it worked?
questions.a: Upside-down bottles with tiny holes drip water slowly; when Leo came home the soil was damp and the plants were healthy.

sessions.title: Hana Slows Down
paragraphs: Hana joined the chess club in the fall and quickly fell in love with the game. She liked how each piece moved in its own way, like the knight jumping in an L shape. When her teacher announced a tournament in December, Hana signed up right away.

During practice games, though, Hana kept losing pieces. She would spot a great move and slide her piece across the board in a flash. A moment later, her opponent would capture her queen or her rook. Hana knew every rule, but she kept making mistakes she could have avoided.

First, Hana decided that she simply needed more practice. She played game after game against her friend Marcus at lunch, but she lost most of them in exactly the same way. Then she memorized the opening moves from a book, but once the game moved past them, she rushed again.

So one evening, Hana played a game with her grandpa, who had played chess for many years. He watched her move quickly and lose a knight. Then he asked, "Before you moved, did you check what my pieces could do?" Hana admitted she had not, so Grandpa told her to count to ten and look for danger first.

It felt strange at first, but Hana followed his advice in every practice game that month. Before each move, she paused and asked herself what her opponent could attack. She started noticing traps before she walked into them. Her games took longer, but she lost far fewer pieces.

Finally, the day of the tournament arrived. Hana stayed calm and checked the board before every move. She won three of her four games and earned a small silver medal. In the end, Hana realized that the secret was not moving fast but taking the time to think.

stops.question: What is Hana's problem, and what is causing it?
stops.lookFor: She keeps losing pieces because she moves too quickly without checking the board.

stops.question: Why didn't more practice or the book of openings fix the problem?
stops.lookFor: They did not change the real cause, which was rushing, so she kept making the same mistakes.

stops.question: How does Grandpa's question help Hana understand the real cause?
stops.lookFor: It makes her realize she was not checking what his pieces could do before she moved.

questions.q: What are the events Hana tries because of her problem?
questions.a: She practices more with Marcus, reads a book of openings, and then asks Grandpa for help.

questions.q: What is the solution?
questions.a: She pauses, counts to ten, and checks for danger before every move.

questions.q: How does the end of the story connect back to the problem?
questions.a: The problem was moving too fast, and the solution was slowing down to think, which helped her win.

sessions.title: Where Is Peanut?
paragraphs: Miss Rivera's third grade class had a fluffy golden hamster named Peanut, who lived in a cage by the window. Every week, a different student got to be the Peanut Helper. This week it was Jayden's turn, and he took the job very seriously. He fed Peanut and always made sure the cage door was latched.

On Monday morning, Jayden hurried to the cage to say hello. His heart sank. The door was open, and the nest of shavings was empty. Someone must have forgotten to close the door after cleaning on Friday. The classroom was big, and a hamster is very small.

First, the whole class searched the room. They peeked under desks and behind the bookshelves, but there was no sign of Peanut. Then Jayden left a few sunflower seeds near the cage. The next morning the seeds were gone, but nobody knew where Peanut had gone afterward.

So Jayden asked his teacher if they could try a science idea he had read about. Hamsters are most active at night, he explained. They needed a way to see where Peanut went while everyone was home. They sprinkled flour around a pile of seeds. In the morning, tiny footprints led straight to the reading corner.

Following the footprints, the class found a small gap behind the beanbag chairs. Jayden placed a shoebox there with soft shavings and a few seeds inside. He tipped it on its side so that Peanut could walk right in. Then everyone went quietly back to their seats.

Finally, after lunch, Jayden tiptoed over to check the shoebox. Peanut was curled up inside, sound asleep on the shavings. The class cheered in whispers so they would not wake him. In the end, Jayden carried Peanut gently back to his cage and checked the latch twice.

stops.question: Why does the author tell us that Jayden takes his job very seriously?
stops.lookFor: It shows why he cares so much about the problem and why he works so hard to solve it.

stops.question: What caused the problem in this story?
stops.lookFor: Someone left the cage door open after cleaning on Friday, so Peanut got out.

stops.question: How does the fact that hamsters are active at night connect to Jayden's plan?
stops.lookFor: Peanut moves when nobody is there, so the flour shows his footprints from the night.

questions.q: What is the problem in this story?
questions.a: Peanut the class hamster escapes from his cage and is lost in the classroom.

questions.q: Why did the flour work better than the seeds alone?
questions.a: The seeds only showed Peanut came to eat; the flour showed footprints of where he went.

questions.q: How does the last sentence connect to what caused the problem?
questions.a: The door was left open before, so Jayden checks the latch twice to make sure it does not happen again.

sessions.title: The Rainy Art Fair
paragraphs: Every spring, Sofia's neighborhood held an art fair in the park on Maple Street. Families set up tables to show paintings, clay bowls, and handmade bracelets. This year, Sofia was in charge of the kids' table. She had spent weeks painting rocks and making paper flowers to share.

Two days before the fair, Sofia checked the weather with her mom. A big rainstorm was expected on Saturday, the exact day of the fair. Sofia's stomach dropped. Paper flowers would turn soggy, and wet paintings would be ruined. The whole fair might have to be called off.

First, Sofia hoped the forecast would change, so she checked it again every few hours. Each time, it still showed dark clouds and heavy rain. Then the neighbors set up a few tents in the park. But there were only three, and that was not nearly enough to cover all the tables.

So Sofia went with her mom to talk to the principal of the school down the street. Sofia explained the problem and asked whether the fair could use the school building. The principal thought about it for a moment. Then she said the gym was empty on weekends and had plenty of room.

On Friday evening, neighbors carried tables, art, and decorations into the gym. Sofia hung her paper flowers along the walls, and the music teacher brought a small speaker. By the time they finished, the gym looked bright and cheerful, even though the sky outside was gray.

Finally, Saturday arrived, and the rain poured down just as the forecast had said. Inside, everything stayed dry. More people came than ever before. Nobody had much else to do on such a rainy day. In the end, the storm that almost ruined the fair helped make it the best one yet.

stops.question: How does the weather forecast change the story here?
stops.lookFor: It creates the problem: rain could ruin the art and cancel the fair.

stops.question: Why do you think the author included the tents that were not enough?
stops.lookFor: It shows a try that only partly worked, so the problem is still not solved and Sofia needs a bigger idea.

stops.question: How does this paragraph connect to Sofia's talk with the principal?
stops.lookFor: Because she said yes, the neighbors can move the fair into the gym; it is the result of her asking.

questions.q: What is the problem and what caused it?
questions.a: A rainstorm was coming on the day of the outdoor fair, which could ruin the art.

questions.q: What tries happened before the solution?
questions.a: Sofia kept checking the forecast, and the neighbors set up tents, but there were not enough.

questions.q: How did the problem turn into something good in the end?
questions.a: The fair moved into the gym, and because of the rain, more people came than ever.

sessions.title: Maya Plants a Garden
paragraphs: Maya wants to grow a garden in the backyard. Mom says it will take a lot of steps. First, they look for a good spot. It needs to get plenty of sun. They pick a place by the back fence. Then Maya pulls out all the weeds. She tugs and tugs until the dirt is bare.

Next, they dig up the dirt. Mom digs with a big spade. Maya digs with a small one. They work until the dirt is soft and loose. Then Maya pokes holes in a long row with her thumb. Mom says the holes should not be too deep. Maya counts out loud as she pokes.

After that, Maya drops the seeds into the holes. She puts two tiny seeds in each one. Mom shows her how to cover them with dirt. Maya pats the dirt down gently. She does not pat too hard. Now the seeds are snug in their little beds.

Then it is time to water the garden. Maya fills the watering can at the tap. It is heavy, so Mom helps her lift it. They sprinkle water over each row. The dirt turns dark and wet. Maya puts a stick at the end of each row. Each stick has the name of a plant on it.

Later, Maya checks the garden every single day. A whole week goes by, and nothing happens. Then one morning she sees tiny green tips. Soon the tips grow into leaves. Finally, the plants grow tall. Maya picks a plump green bean. All of the steps were worth it!

stops.question: Why do Maya and Mom pull out the weeds before they dig?
stops.lookFor: The weeds have to go first so the dirt is clear; you cannot dig a neat garden with weeds in the way.

stops.question: What would happen if Maya watered the dirt before she put in the seeds and covered them?
stops.lookFor: The seeds would not get the water, or the water would be wasted; the seeds need to be in the dirt first so the water can reach them.

stops.question: The seeds are planted and watered. What clue words do you think will come next to show a long time passing?
stops.lookFor: Words like later, after a while, or one day; growing takes time, so the author needs words that show days going by.

questions.q: What was the very first step, and why did it have to come first?
questions.a: Finding a sunny spot, because they needed a place for the garden before they could weed, dig, or plant.

questions.q: Which time words did the author use to show the order of the steps?
questions.a: First, next, then, after that, later, and finally.

questions.q: How did the author show that many days passed at the end?
questions.a: She used later, a week goes by, and one day, and showed the plants change from tips to leaves to tall plants.

sessions.title: Sunday Pancakes
paragraphs: Leo and Grandpa make pancakes every Sunday morning. First, Leo washes his hands with soap. Grandpa ties an apron on him. It is much too big, so they roll up the ends. Then Grandpa gets out a big bowl. Leo sets out a cup and a spoon.

Next, Leo adds the flour. When he scoops it out with the cup, a puff of white dust flies up. Leo sneezes, and Grandpa laughs. Then Grandpa cracks two eggs into the bowl. Leo pours in the milk very slowly so it does not spill.

After that, Leo mixes it all up. He stirs and stirs with the big spoon. At first the batter has lots of lumps, but Grandpa tells him to keep going. Soon it is smooth and thick. Leo's arm is tired, but he does not stop. At last the batter is done.

Then Grandpa heats the pan on the stove. Leo stands back to stay safe. Grandpa adds a bit of butter, and it melts and hisses. He pours a scoop of batter into the pan. They watch for little bubbles on top. When the bubbles pop, it is time to flip.

Grandpa lets Leo hold the flipper with him. One, two, three, flip! The pancake lands with a soft plop, and it is golden brown. They make a tall stack this way. Finally, Leo adds a pat of butter and a drip of syrup. He takes a big bite and smiles.

stops.question: Why does Leo wash his hands before he touches any food?
stops.lookFor: Clean hands come first so germs do not get in the food; it is a step you do before cooking starts.

stops.question: Why does Leo have to mix the batter before Grandpa can heat the pan?
stops.lookFor: The batter has to be ready first; you cannot cook pancakes until there is smooth batter to pour in.

stops.question: What clue told Grandpa and Leo that it was time for the next step?
stops.lookFor: The bubbles popping on top showed the pancake was ready to flip; one step tells you when the next one starts.

questions.q: What steps did Leo do to make the batter, in order?
questions.a: He added the flour, Grandpa cracked the eggs, Leo poured the milk, and then he mixed until it was smooth.

questions.q: What would go wrong if they tried to flip the pancake before the bubbles popped?
questions.a: It would still be runny and would fall apart or splat, because it was not cooked enough yet.

questions.q: Which words helped you know what came next in the story?
questions.a: First, then, next, after that, and finally.

sessions.title: Bath Time for Biscuit
paragraphs: Biscuit the dog rolled in the mud. Now he is a brown mess! Nia and Dad must give him a bath. First, Nia gets the things they need. She grabs dog soap, a brush, and two old towels. Dad fills the tub with warm water. He checks it with his hand to make sure it is not too hot.

Next, Dad lifts Biscuit into the tub. Biscuit does not like it at first, so he shakes and sends drops all over. Nia giggles and pets him. She talks to him in a calm voice until he sits still. Then she pours cups of water on his back until his fur is wet.

After that, Nia rubs in the soap and makes lots of white suds. She scrubs his back, his legs, and his tail. Dad washes his face with care to keep the soap out of his eyes. The mud starts to slide off, and the water in the tub turns brown.

Then it is time to rinse. Dad lets out the dirty water, and Nia pours clean water on Biscuit. She rinses and rinses. Any soap left on him will make his skin itch. At last the water runs clear. Biscuit looks thin and wet and a little silly.

Now Dad lifts Biscuit out, and Nia wraps him in a towel. She rubs him dry while he gives one more big shake. Then Nia brushes his fur until it is soft and fluffy. Finally, Biscuit is clean! He runs out to the yard. Nia hopes he stays out of the mud this time.

stops.question: Why does Nia get the soap and towels ready before Biscuit goes in the tub?
stops.lookFor: So everything is close by; once a wet dog is in the tub, you cannot leave to go find things.

stops.question: Why does Nia make Biscuit's fur wet before she puts on the soap?
stops.lookFor: Soap works on wet fur and makes suds; wetting him first gets him ready for the next step.

stops.question: What would happen if they dried Biscuit before they rinsed off all the soap?
stops.lookFor: The soap would stay in his fur and his skin would itch; rinsing has to come before drying.

questions.q: What made the whole bath happen in the first place?
questions.a: Biscuit rolled in the mud, so he needed a bath.

questions.q: How did the water change as the steps went on?
questions.a: It was warm and clean at first, turned brown when the mud came off, and ran clear after the rinse.

questions.q: Which word tells you the bath is all done?
questions.a: Finally.

sessions.title: Jordan's Birdhouse
paragraphs: Jordan wanted to build a birdhouse for the tree in his yard. His mom said they could make one together on Saturday. First, they looked at a plan in a book. The plan showed every piece they would need. Jordan counted six parts. There was a floor, a back, a front, two sides, and a roof.

Next, Mom helped Jordan measure the wood. He used a ruler and a pencil to mark each line. Mom cut the boards with a saw while Jordan watched from a safe spot. Then Jordan sanded every piece. He rubbed until the edges felt smooth. No bird would get a splinter in his house.

After that, it was time to put the parts together. Jordan held the sides up straight. Mom tapped in small nails with a hammer. They added the floor and the back. Then Jordan drilled a round hole in the front piece with Mom's help. That hole would be the door for the birds.

Once the front was on, they set the roof on top. It tipped down so rain would slide off. Mom nailed it in place. Jordan gave the whole house a shake. Nothing wiggled or fell off. It was strong and ready for paint.

Later that day, Jordan painted the birdhouse sky blue. He had to wait for the paint to dry before he could hang it. The next morning, Mom held the ladder while Jordan hung it on a branch. Finally, they sat by the window to watch. A small brown bird hopped to the door and peeked inside.

stops.question: Why did Jordan sand every piece before they nailed the birdhouse together?
stops.lookFor: Sanding is easier on flat, loose pieces, and it had to be done before building so the edges were smooth for the birds.

stops.question: How did nailing the sides, floor, and back first help with the next steps?
stops.lookFor: It made a strong box, so the front and roof had something to attach to.

stops.question: What would go wrong if Jordan tried to hang the birdhouse before the roof was nailed on?
stops.lookFor: The roof could fall off or rain could get in; the house had to be finished and strong before it went in the tree.

questions.q: Why did Jordan and Mom look at a plan before cutting any wood?
questions.a: So they knew what pieces they needed and how big to make them before they started.

questions.q: What step made Jordan wait, and what words show the time passing?
questions.a: Painting, because the paint had to dry; the words later that day and the next morning show time passing.

questions.q: Retell the main steps of building the birdhouse in order.
questions.a: Look at the plan, measure and cut, sand, nail the parts together, add the roof, paint, and hang it.

sessions.topic: getting ready for a soccer game
sessions.title: Amara's First Game
paragraphs: Amara had her very first soccer game on Saturday morning. The night before, she laid out her uniform on a chair. She put her red shirt, black shorts, and long socks in a neat pile. Then she packed her bag with a water bottle and her shin guards. She went to bed early so she would not be tired.

In the morning, Amara woke up before her alarm. First, she ate a bowl of oatmeal with bananas. Dad said food would give her the power to run. Next, she got dressed. She slid on the shin guards first. Then she pulled her long socks up over them. Last, she laced her cleats and tied a double knot.

After that, the family drove to the park. Amara's team met at the far field. The coach had them warm up together. They jogged two laps around the cones. Then they stretched their legs and arms. Amara felt her heart thump fast. She was excited and a little nervous, too.

Next, the coach gave them a quick talk. She told them to pass the ball and cheer for each other. The players put their hands in a circle. They shouted their team name. Then the whistle blew, and the game began. Amara ran onto the field with her friends.

During the game, Amara passed the ball to her teammate Zoe. Zoe kicked it right into the net. The team cheered loudly. At the end, both teams lined up and slapped hands. Finally, Amara drank her whole water bottle. Getting ready had been a lot of work, but it helped her play her best.

stops.question: Why do you think Amara packed her bag the night before instead of in the morning?
stops.lookFor: So she would not rush or forget things in the morning; getting ready early made the next day easier.

stops.question: Why did Amara have to put on her shin guards before her socks?
stops.lookFor: The socks go over the shin guards to hold them in place; if the order were switched, the guards would not stay on.

stops.question: What happened right before the whistle blew, and how did it get the team ready?
stops.lookFor: The coach gave a talk and they cheered their team name, which helped them feel ready to work together.

questions.q: How did getting ready the night before help Amara the next morning?
questions.a: Her things were already laid out and packed, so she could just eat, dress, and go.

questions.q: Why did the team warm up before the game instead of after?
questions.a: Warming up gets bodies ready to run so they can play well; after the game it would be too late.

questions.q: Find two words or phrases that show the order of events.
questions.a: Any two of: the night before, in the morning, first, next, then, last, after that, during the game, at the end, finally.

sessions.title: The Snow Day Snowman
paragraphs: Theo looked out the window and saw a yard covered in white. It was a snow day! First, he and his sister Ava ate a warm breakfast of eggs and toast. Then they bundled up in snow pants, thick coats, and fuzzy hats. Mom helped them zip up and pull on their mittens. Now they were ready to go outside.

Next, Theo and Ava started on the bottom of the snowman. Theo packed a small snowball in his hands. He set it on the ground and began to roll it. The ball picked up more snow as it went. It grew bigger and bigger. Soon it was too heavy to push alone, so Ava came over to help him.

After that, they made a second ball for the middle. It was a little smaller than the first. They both lifted it together and set it on top. Then Ava rolled the smallest ball for the head. Theo stood on his tiptoes to place it at the very top. Now the snowman had three parts.

Then they gave the snowman a face. Ava found two dark stones for the eyes. Theo ran inside for a carrot to use as a nose. They used small sticks to make a crooked smile. Last, they poked two long branches into the sides for arms. Theo wrapped his old striped scarf around its neck.

Later, their noses were red and their fingers felt cold. Mom called them inside for mugs of hot cocoa. They sat by the window and sipped their drinks. Outside, the snowman seemed to wave at them. Finally, Theo let out a big yawn. It had been a long, happy day in the snow.

stops.question: Why did Theo and Ava bundle up before they went outside?
stops.lookFor: It was cold and snowy; they had to dress warm first or they could not stay out to play.

stops.question: Why do you think they made the biggest ball first?
stops.lookFor: The biggest ball goes on the bottom to hold up the others, so it has to be made and set down first.

stops.question: What would happen if they tried to add the face before they stacked the three balls?
stops.lookFor: There would be no head to put the face on; the body had to be built before the face and arms.

questions.q: What were the main steps for building the snowman, in order?
questions.a: Roll the big bottom ball, add the middle ball, add the head, then add the face, arms, and scarf.

questions.q: How did each snowball compare to the one before it, and why?
questions.a: Each one was smaller, so the bigger ones could hold up the smaller ones on top.

questions.q: Which words show the end of the day?
questions.a: Later, their noses were red, and Finally, Theo yawned.

sessions.topic: building a sandcastle at the beach
sessions.title: The Tallest Sandcastle
paragraphs: Kai and his cousin Lila spent the whole afternoon at the beach, and they had one big goal. They wanted to build the tallest sandcastle anyone had ever seen. First, they had to find the right spot. Sand near the water was wet and easy to shape. Sand too close to the waves would wash away, though. They chose a place halfway between.

Next, they gathered their tools. Lila grabbed two buckets, a shovel, and a plastic cup. Kai found a flat shell to use for smoothing the walls. Then they filled one bucket with seawater. They would need it to keep the sand damp while they worked. Dry sand falls apart, so the water was important.

After that, they started on the base. Kai dug a wide circle and piled the sand in the middle. Lila poured water on the pile and patted it down hard. They kept adding sand and water, layer by layer. Soon they had a strong, flat mound. It was as wide as a car tire.

Then it was time for the towers. Lila packed wet sand into a bucket and flipped it upside down on the mound. She lifted the bucket slowly so the tower stayed in one piece. Kai made smaller towers with the cup. He used the shell to carve windows and doors into each one.

Later, Kai dug a moat around the whole castle. When a wave rolled in, water filled the moat like a little river. Lila stuck a seagull feather on top of the tallest tower like a flag. Finally, they stepped back to admire their work. The castle stood proud in the golden light as the sun went down.

stops.question: Why was choosing the right spot the very first step?
stops.lookFor: Everything else depended on it; in the wrong spot the sand would be too dry to shape or the waves would wash the castle away.

stops.question: How did building a strong, flat base help with the step that came next?
stops.lookFor: The towers needed something solid to stand on; a weak base would make the towers crack or fall.

stops.question: Why did the bucket of water from earlier in the story matter for making the towers?
stops.lookFor: The towers needed wet sand to hold their shape; getting water early set up this later step.

questions.q: What was the order of the main steps Kai and Lila followed?
questions.a: Pick a spot, gather tools and water, build the base, make the towers, then dig the moat and add the flag.

questions.q: What would happen if they tried to build towers before making the base?
questions.a: The towers would sit on loose sand and could tip or fall apart.

questions.q: Which words helped show that the day was ending?
questions.a: Later, finally, and as the sun went down.

sessions.title: The Kitten Takes the Stage
paragraphs: Imani's class was putting on a play about a lost kitten. Tonight was the big show. Imani was the kitten, so she had a lot to do. First, she went over her lines one last time at breakfast. Her brother Malik read the other parts for her. She did not miss a single word.

After school, Imani went to the gym with her class. Next, the teacher had them act out the whole play from start to end. This was called a dress rehearsal. Imani learned where to stand and when to walk on stage. She even found a strip of tape on the floor that marked her spot.

Then it was time to get into costumes. Imani pulled on a soft gray suit with a long tail. A friend helped her put on a headband with fuzzy ears. After that, a mom painted black whiskers on her cheeks. Imani looked in the mirror and grinned. She really looked like a kitten!

Later, families started to fill the seats. Imani peeked out from behind the curtain. She felt butterflies in her tummy. Her teacher told the class to take three deep breaths. They all breathed in and out together. Then the lights went down, and the room got very quiet.

The curtain opened, and the show began. Imani said her first line in a squeaky kitten voice. The crowd laughed. She knew every part, just like she had practiced. At the end, the whole class came out to take a bow. Finally, Imani heard her family cheering the loudest of all.

stops.question: Why did Imani practice her lines in the morning, long before the show?
stops.lookFor: Practicing early helped her remember them later; the morning step got her ready for the night.

stops.question: How do you think the dress rehearsal will help Imani during the real show?
stops.lookFor: She will already know where to stand and when to walk on, because she practiced it all in order first.

stops.question: What clue words have shown time moving closer to the show?
stops.lookFor: After school, then, after that, later, and then the lights went down; each one moves the day closer to the show.

questions.q: How did the practice steps earlier in the day lead to what happened at the end?
questions.a: Because she practiced her lines and the dress rehearsal, she remembered every part during the show.

questions.q: Why did the costumes come after the dress rehearsal and right before the show?
questions.a: The costumes and face paint needed to look fresh for the show, so they came last before the families arrived.

questions.q: Name the order of Imani's day, from morning to night.
questions.a: Practice lines at breakfast, dress rehearsal after school, costumes and whiskers, deep breaths backstage, the show, and the bow.

sessions.title: Building a Town on the Island
paragraphs: Omar and his friend Hana were playing a video game where players build their own island. Today they wanted to make a tiny town for the animals in the game. First, they had to collect supplies. Omar chopped down trees to get wood. Hana dug in a cave and found shiny gray stones. They put everything into a big wooden chest.

Next, they had to pick a good place for the town. The island had hills, a river, and a sandy beach. Hana said that hills would make building hard. So they chose a wide, grassy field near the river. Then Omar cleared away all the bushes so they had plenty of room to work.

After that, they built the houses. Hana used the stones to make strong walls. Omar added wooden roofs and little doors. They made four houses in a row along a path. Each one had a window that glowed yellow when night came in the game. The town was starting to look real.

Then they needed a way to cross the river. Omar placed long planks from one side to the other. He tested the bridge by walking his character all the way across it. It held up, so Hana added a railing. Now the animals could visit the farm on the other side of the water.

Later, they planted a garden of carrots and berries next to the houses. The game animals wandered into their new homes one by one. Hana waved at a pig wearing a tiny hat. Finally, the sun set over their island town. Omar saved the game so they could keep building tomorrow.

stops.question: Why did Omar and Hana collect supplies before they did anything else?
stops.lookFor: They needed wood and stone to build; without supplies first, they could not make the houses later.

stops.question: How did choosing a flat field make the next step easier?
stops.lookFor: Flat ground is easier to build on, so it was ready for the houses; picking the spot set up the building step.

stops.question: Why did Omar test the bridge before Hana added the railing?
stops.lookFor: They had to know the bridge was strong first; there is no point adding a railing to a bridge that might break.

questions.q: What were the main steps of building the town, in order?
questions.a: Collect supplies, pick a spot, build the houses, build the bridge, then plant a garden.

questions.q: Which step used the supplies they collected at the start?
questions.a: Building the houses, because Hana used the stones for walls and Omar used wood for roofs and doors.

questions.q: What words tell you the building session is ending?
questions.a: Later, finally, the sun set, and Omar saved the game to keep building tomorrow.

sessions.title: Bread for the Firefighters
paragraphs: Sofia's grandma had a plan to thank the firefighters at the station down the street. They would bake two loaves of warm, fresh bread. Then they would deliver them by hand. First, Sofia read the recipe card out loud. Grandma set everything on the counter. There was flour, yeast, salt, sugar, and a jug of warm water.

Next, Grandma showed Sofia how to wake up the yeast. They stirred it into the warm water with a spoonful of sugar. Then they waited ten minutes until the mixture turned foamy on top. Grandma explained that the foam meant the yeast was alive and ready to work. Without that step, the bread would stay flat.

After that, Sofia poured the foamy water into the bowl of flour and salt. She mixed it all with her hands. Soon it became a sticky ball of dough. Then she kneaded it on the counter, pushing and folding it over and over. Her arms got tired, but the dough grew smooth and stretchy.

Then came the hardest part, which was waiting. They placed the dough in a bowl and covered it with a clean towel. For an hour, it sat in a warm corner. Slowly it puffed up to twice its size. Sofia peeked under the towel three times. When it was ready, Grandma shaped it into two loaves.

Later, the loaves baked in the oven until their tops were golden brown. The whole kitchen smelled wonderful. Once the bread had cooled, Sofia wrapped each loaf in a cloth. She tied it with string. Finally, she and Grandma walked to the fire station. The firefighters smiled and thanked them for the tasty surprise.

stops.question: Why did they have to wait for the yeast to foam before mixing it with the flour?
stops.lookFor: The foam showed the yeast was alive; if they skipped ahead, the bread would not rise and would stay flat.

stops.question: What would happen if Sofia skipped the kneading and went straight to baking?
stops.lookFor: The dough would not get smooth and stretchy, so the bread would not turn out right; each step gets the dough ready for the next.

stops.question: What words tell you how much time passed while the dough rose?
stops.lookFor: For an hour, slowly, and Sofia peeked three times, which show a long wait before the next step.

questions.q: Why did Sofia read the recipe before doing anything else?
questions.a: The recipe told them what they needed and the order of the steps, so reading it first helped them do everything right.

questions.q: How did waking up the yeast early in the story connect to the dough puffing up later?
questions.a: The live yeast is what made the dough rise to twice its size during the waiting step.

questions.q: Why did Sofia wait for the bread to cool before wrapping it?
questions.a: Hot bread could get soggy or be hard to handle; cooling had to come before wrapping and delivering.

sessions.title: Fossil Day at Camp
paragraphs: Eli had been waiting all summer for Fossil Day at science camp. Each camper would get to dig for dinosaur bones in a giant sandbox. The bones were only models. Still, the leaders had buried them just like real fossils. First, the leader handed out tools. Eli got a small trowel, a soft brush, and a notebook.

Next, the leader explained how to dig with care. Real fossil hunters never just grab a bone and pull it out. Instead, they scrape away a thin layer of dirt at a time. Then they sweep the loose dirt aside with a brush. Eli knelt in his square of sand and began to scrape very slowly.

After about twenty minutes, Eli's trowel hit something hard. He set the trowel down right away and picked up the brush. Then he swept gently around the edges. Soon a curved shape appeared. It looked like part of a giant rib bone! His heart pounded, but he kept his hands steady.

Before he lifted anything, Eli had to record his find. He drew a sketch of the bone in his notebook. Next, he measured it with a ruler. He wrote down where it was in his square. The leader said scientists take notes first so they remember where each fossil was found.

After that, Eli lifted the rib with care and placed it on a tray. By the end of the morning, the campers had dug up a whole skeleton. They worked together to lay the pieces in order on a long table. Finally, everyone stood back and stared. A model dinosaur almost as long as a school bus stretched out in front of them.

stops.question: Why do fossil hunters scrape away one thin layer at a time instead of digging fast?
stops.lookFor: Going slowly keeps them from breaking a bone they cannot see yet; each careful layer comes before the next.

stops.question: Why did Eli switch from the trowel to the brush once he touched something hard?
stops.lookFor: The trowel could scratch or crack the bone, so finding it led to a gentler step with the brush.

stops.question: What would be lost if Eli lifted the bone before he drew and measured it?
stops.lookFor: No one would know exactly where it had been found; once it is moved, that information is gone.

questions.q: List the steps of a careful fossil dig in the order Eli did them.
questions.a: Scrape thin layers, brush away dirt, uncover the shape, sketch and measure it, then lift it onto a tray.

questions.q: Which phrases show how time passed during the dig?
questions.a: After about twenty minutes, before he lifted anything, after that, by the end of the morning, and finally.

questions.q: How did each camper's careful work lead to the ending?
questions.a: Because everyone dug and recorded their bones carefully, they could put the pieces in order and build a whole skeleton.

sessions.title: The Cardboard Rocket
paragraphs: Zoe and her little brother Ben found a huge cardboard box in the garage after their family got a new fridge. Zoe had an idea right away. They would build a rocket and fly it to the moon, at least in their imaginations. First, they dragged the box into the backyard and stood it up on one end.

Next, they planned the rocket on paper. Zoe drew a tall shape with a pointed top and fins at the bottom. Ben added a round window so they could see the stars. Then they gathered supplies from the craft bin, including tape, markers, paper plates, and an old flashlight. Mom helped them cut a door in the side.

After that, they built the nose cone. Zoe rolled a big piece of poster board into a cone and taped it to the top of the box. Ben taped two paper plates inside for control buttons. Then they cut triangle fins from the leftover cardboard and taped them near the ground so the rocket would look balanced.

Once the rocket was built, they painted it silver and wrote their mission name on the side. They had to wait an hour for the paint to dry before they could climb in. While they waited, Ben made a checklist for launch. It said helmets, snacks, flashlight, and a map of the moon.

Finally, it was launch time. The two astronauts squeezed inside with their bike helmets on. Ben flipped on the flashlight, and Zoe began the countdown from ten. When she reached zero, they shook the box and shouted. Moments later, they peeked out the round window and pretended they could see Earth far below.

stops.question: Why did Zoe and Ben plan the rocket on paper before they started cutting and taping?
stops.lookFor: A plan showed what parts they needed and where they went, so the building steps would go in the right order.

stops.question: What would have happened if they had painted the rocket before taping on the nose cone and fins?
stops.lookFor: The new parts would not be painted, or wet paint would get messed up; building had to come before painting.

stops.question: Why did the paint step make them wait, and how did they use that time?
stops.lookFor: The paint had to dry before they could climb in, so Ben made a launch checklist while they waited.

questions.q: What were the main steps Zoe and Ben followed to build the rocket?
questions.a: Stand up the box, plan on paper, gather supplies and cut a door, add the nose cone, buttons, and fins, then paint it.

questions.q: How did the round window Ben drew in the plan show up again at the end?
questions.a: At the end they peeked out the round window and pretended to see Earth, so an early idea paid off later.

questions.q: Which words show that the launch happened last?
questions.a: Finally, it was launch time, followed by the countdown and moments later.

sessions.topic: starting a band for a talent show
sessions.title: The Three-Week Band
paragraphs: When Marcus saw the poster for the school talent show, he knew he wanted to play with a band. The show was only three weeks away, so he had to plan carefully. First, he asked his friends Jayden and Hana to join. Jayden played drums on a practice pad. Hana had taken keyboard lessons since kindergarten.

Next, the three friends had to choose a song. They sat together at lunch and wrote a list of ideas on a napkin. After a long talk, they picked a cheerful song about summer. Then Hana wrote out the chords. That way, all three of them could practice the same version at home.

During the first week, they practiced on their own, because each person had a separate part to learn. Marcus strummed his guitar every night until his fingertips felt sore. In the second week, they met in Jayden's garage to play together. It sounded messy at first. Everyone was playing at a slightly different speed.

To fix the problem, Jayden offered to count them in and keep a steady beat. After that, the song started to come together. By the end of the second week, they could play it all the way through without stopping. In the third week, they played for their families to get used to an audience.

Finally, the night of the talent show arrived. The friends waited backstage while other students sang, danced, and juggled. When their names were called, they walked out and took their places. Jayden clicked his sticks four times, and the music began. As the last chord rang out, the crowd cheered. Marcus grinned at his bandmates.

stops.question: Why did Hana write out the chords before anyone started practicing at home?
stops.lookFor: So everyone learned the same version; if they practiced first, they might each learn it differently.

stops.question: The author says during the first week and in the second week instead of just next. How do those phrases help you follow the story?
stops.lookFor: They show exactly how much time passed and that the plan moved week by week toward the show.

stops.question: How did the messy first practice lead to the next step?
