stops.lookFor: Because they played at different speeds, Jayden started counting them in and keeping the beat, which fixed the problem.

questions.q: Why did Marcus need to find bandmates before choosing a song?
questions.a: The song had to work for the instruments and people in the band, so he needed to know who was in it first.

questions.q: What would have happened if the band had skipped practicing in front of their families?
questions.a: They might have been more nervous or made mistakes on stage, because they would not be used to an audience.

questions.q: Retell the three-week plan in order.
questions.a: Week one they practiced alone, week two they played together and fixed the beat, week three they played for their families, then came the show.

sessions.title: Lemonade for the Shelter
paragraphs: Rosa and her neighbor Mateo wanted to help the animal shelter in their town. They hoped to raise money for toys and blankets. After thinking about it all afternoon, they decided to open a lemonade stand on Saturday. First, they asked their parents if it was okay. Then they picked a shady spot at the corner. Lots of people walked their dogs there.

Next, they made a shopping list. They needed lemons, sugar, ice, cups, and a big pitcher with a lid. Rosa's dad drove them to the store, where they chose the cheapest bag of lemons. Back at home, they made a sign out of poster board. It said that all of the money would go to the shelter.

On Saturday morning, they started by squeezing the lemons. Mateo rolled each lemon on the counter first, because that made the juice flow out more easily. Rosa squeezed them over a strainer to catch the seeds. After that, they stirred the juice with water and sugar. They tasted it until it was sweet but still a little sour.

Then they carried everything to the corner. They set up a folding table and taped the sign to the front. They filled the pitcher with ice so the lemonade would stay cold. Their first customer was a woman walking a fluffy white dog. She bought two cups and said she loved their reason for selling lemonade.

As the morning went on, the line grew longer. They had to make a second pitcher. Later that afternoon, they counted their money and found they had earned forty dollars. Finally, on Monday, they brought a bag of new toys and blankets to the shelter. A helper there let them watch a puppy chew on a squeaky bone.

stops.question: Why did Rosa and Mateo ask their parents before doing anything else?
stops.lookFor: They needed permission before the plan could go forward; without a yes, none of the other steps could happen.

stops.question: Why did Mateo roll the lemons before Rosa squeezed them?
stops.lookFor: Rolling them first made the juice come out more easily, so one step made the next step work better.

stops.question: How did the sign they made earlier help with their first customer?
stops.lookFor: The sign told people the money was for the shelter, and the first customer said she loved that reason.

questions.q: Why did they make a shopping list before going to the store?
questions.a: So they would know exactly what to buy and would not forget anything they needed.

questions.q: Which phrases show the days and times in the story?
questions.a: After a whole afternoon, on Saturday morning, as the morning went on, later in the afternoon, and finally, on Monday.

questions.q: How did selling lemonade lead to the ending of the story?
questions.a: The money they earned paid for the toys and blankets they brought to the shelter.

sessions.topic: inventing a robot for the science fair
sessions.title: The Scribble Robot
paragraphs: For the school science fair, Priya decided to build a robot that could draw pictures all by itself. Her older cousin Noah, who loved inventing things, offered to help her. First, they watched a short video that explained how a scribble robot works. The robot would shake as it moved. Markers taped to its legs would leave colorful lines.

Next, they gathered the parts they needed. They used a plastic cup for the body, three markers for legs, a small motor, a battery pack, and a cork. Noah explained that the motor alone would just spin smoothly. But if they pushed the cork onto the motor a little off center, the whole robot would wobble across the paper.

Then they started building. Priya turned the cup upside down and taped the three markers around the outside. The caps pointed up, and the tips touched the table. After that, Noah helped her tape the motor and the battery pack to the top of the cup. Then they pressed the cork onto the end of the motor.

Before testing the robot, they spread a large sheet of paper on the floor. They pulled the caps off all three markers. When Priya hooked up the wires, the robot buzzed loudly and began to shake. It slid across the paper in wobbly circles, leaving loops of blue, green, and orange. Priya laughed so hard that she nearly fell over.

At the science fair the next week, Priya set her robot on a table. Beside it was a big poster that showed each step of how she built it. Many visitors watched the robot draw and asked how it worked. Priya proudly explained the off-center cork. Finally, at the end of the day, the judges gave her a ribbon for the most creative project.

stops.question: Why did Priya and Noah learn how a scribble robot works before they gathered any parts?
stops.lookFor: Knowing how it works told them which parts to get and why; learning had to come before building.

stops.question: How does the off-center cork explain what will happen in a later step?
stops.lookFor: The cork makes the robot wobble, so when it is turned on it will shake and move across the paper.

stops.question: What would have happened if Priya connected the wires before taking the caps off the markers?
stops.lookFor: The robot would shake but leave no lines, so the test would not show it drawing; the caps had to come off first.

questions.q: What were the building steps, in order?
questions.a: Tape markers to the cup, attach the motor and battery, press the cork on, then take off the caps and connect the wires.

questions.q: Why did Priya put a poster showing each step at the science fair?
questions.a: The steps explained how she built it, so visitors and judges could follow her work in order.

questions.q: Which words show time passing between building the robot and winning the ribbon?
questions.a: At the science fair the following week, and finally, at the end of the day.

sessions.title: The First-Night Box
paragraphs: When Jada learned that her family was moving across town, she felt both excited and a little worried. She did not want to leave her old bedroom behind. Her parents promised that moving day would go smoothly if everyone followed a plan. First, two weeks before the move, the family sorted through every closet and drawer in the house.

Next, they decided what to keep, what to give away, and what to throw out. Jada filled a whole box with toys she had outgrown. Her mother drove it to a center that gives things to families in need. Then the packing began. Jada wrapped her favorite books in newspaper and labeled each box with the name of its room.

On the night before the move, the family packed a special box called the first-night box. Inside it, they placed toothbrushes, pajamas, a flashlight, snacks, and clean sheets. Her father explained that this box would ride in the car instead of the truck. That way, they would not have to dig through dozens of boxes when they arrived.

Early the next morning, a moving truck pulled up in front of the house. The movers carried the heaviest furniture first so the large pieces could go against the walls of the truck. Then they loaded the boxes around them. Afterward, Jada walked through her empty bedroom one last time and whispered goodbye.

Later that afternoon, the truck arrived at the new house. The labels on each box helped the movers carry them to the correct rooms. Jada unpacked her books first and lined them up on her new shelf. Finally, as the sun went down, the family opened the first-night box. They made the beds and shared a picnic dinner on the living room floor.

stops.question: Why did the family sort and give things away before they started packing?
stops.lookFor: Getting rid of things first meant fewer boxes to pack and move; sorting made the packing step easier.

stops.question: Why do you think the first-night box was packed last, on the night before the move?
stops.lookFor: It held things they needed every day, like toothbrushes and pajamas, so it had to be packed at the very end.

stops.question: Why did the movers load the heaviest furniture before the boxes?
stops.lookFor: The big pieces needed to go against the truck walls first, then the boxes could fit around them; switching the order would not work.

questions.q: How did labeling the boxes early in the story help later?
questions.a: When the truck arrived, the labels showed the movers which room each box belonged in.

questions.q: What time phrases did the author use to move the story forward?
questions.a: Two weeks before the move, on the night before the move, early the next morning, afterward, later that afternoon, and as the sun went down.

questions.q: How did the first-night box connect the beginning of moving day to the end?
questions.a: It was packed before the move and opened at the end, so the family had everything they needed on the first night.

sessions.title: The Bike in the Shed
paragraphs: Isaac found an old blue bicycle hidden behind the lawn mower in his grandfather's shed. It was covered in dust and cobwebs. The neighborhood bike parade was only a week away, and Isaac wondered if this forgotten bike could be ready in time. Grandpa studied it closely. He said they could fix it, but only if they did each repair in the right order.

First, they washed the whole bicycle with soapy water and an old toothbrush, because it is hard to find problems hiding under thick dirt. Once the frame was shining, they could see what needed work. The chain was rusty, and both tires were flat. The brakes squeaked loudly whenever Isaac squeezed the handles.

Next, they worked on the tires. Grandpa showed Isaac how to take off each wheel and look for tiny holes in the rubber tubes. They found one small hole, patched it, and pumped both tires full of air. After that, they scrubbed the rust off the chain with a wire brush. Then they added a few drops of oil so it would move smoothly.

The brakes came last, because Grandpa said they needed the wheels back on to test them. Isaac tightened the brake cables while his grandfather spun each wheel and squeezed the handles. They checked that the pads gripped evenly on both sides. Then Isaac rode slowly up and down the driveway, stopping again and again until he trusted the brakes.

On the morning of the parade, Isaac tied colorful streamers to the handlebars and clipped a small bell to the front. Finally, he joined the other riders at the end of the street. He rang his bell as the parade rolled past cheering neighbors. His grandfather waved from the sidewalk, proud of the patient work they had finished together.

stops.question: Grandpa says the repairs must be done in the right order. Why might the order matter when fixing a bike?
stops.lookFor: Some jobs depend on others being done first; doing them out of order could mean redoing work or missing problems.

stops.question: Why did cleaning the bike have to come before any repairs?
stops.lookFor: Dirt hid the problems; only after cleaning could they see the rusty chain, flat tires, and squeaky brakes.

stops.question: What might go wrong if they had oiled the chain before scrubbing off the rust?
stops.lookFor: The oil would mix with the rust and dirt, and the chain still would not move smoothly; scrubbing had to come first.

questions.q: Why did the brakes have to wait until after the wheels were fixed?
questions.a: They needed the wheels back on to spin them and test whether the brakes gripped evenly.

questions.q: List the repairs in the order Isaac and Grandpa did them.
questions.a: Clean the bike, fix and fill the tires, clean and oil the chain, then adjust and test the brakes.

questions.q: How did the deadline in the first paragraph shape the rest of the story?
questions.a: The parade was a week away, so they had to work step by step to finish in time, and the story ends at the parade.

sessions.topic: a family hike to a waterfall
sessions.title: The Trail to Silver Falls
paragraphs: Elena and her older brother Sam had begged their parents for months to hike the trail to Silver Falls. When the weekend finally came, the family started getting ready the evening before. First, they checked the weather report to make sure no storms were coming. Then they packed water, sandwiches, sunscreen, and a first aid kit.

The next morning, they drove to the park and stopped at the ranger station. A friendly ranger handed them a trail map. She reminded them to stay on the marked path to protect the plants. Then the family studied the map together, tracing the route with their fingers. The waterfall was about two miles away, at the top of a long, winding climb.

After the first mile, the trail grew steep and rocky, and Elena's legs began to ache. Her father said they should rest on a fallen log, drink some water, and eat some trail mix. While they rested, Sam spotted a hawk circling high above the trees. Feeling fresh again, the family kept climbing, following the painted marks on the trees.

Soon they heard a low, rushing sound that grew louder around each bend. Elena ran ahead and gasped when she saw the waterfall tumbling over a cliff into a clear pool. The family ate their sandwiches on a flat rock beside the pool. Cool mist drifted over them. Sam took photos so they could remember the view.

Later that afternoon, the family began the long walk back down the trail. Going downhill felt much easier. They checked the map at every fork so they would not take a wrong turn. Finally, they reached the car just as the sun dipped behind the mountains. Elena fell asleep on the drive home, dreaming about the sparkling waterfall.

stops.question: Why did the family check the weather before packing their bags?
stops.lookFor: If storms were coming, they might not go at all, and the weather helps decide what to pack; checking came first for a reason.

stops.question: How did resting and drinking water help the family with the next part of the hike?
stops.lookFor: It gave them energy to keep climbing the steep trail; the rest made the next step possible.

stops.question: What clue told Elena the waterfall was close before she could see it?
stops.lookFor: The rushing sound that grew louder around each bend; the sound came first and led her to run ahead and find it.

questions.q: How did getting the map at the ranger station help at the end of the story?
questions.a: On the way down, they checked the map at every fork so they would not take a wrong turn.

questions.q: Which phrases show the time of day changing throughout the story?
questions.a: The evening before, the next morning, after the first mile, soon, later that afternoon, and as the sun dipped behind the mountains.

questions.q: Why did the author tell the trip in time order from start to finish?
questions.a: So readers could follow the family step by step, from getting ready, to the climb, to the waterfall, and back home.

sessions.title: Why Leaves Change Color
paragraphs: Leaves are green in spring and summer. Why? They are full of a green color called chlorophyll. It helps a leaf make food from sunlight. A tree needs that food to grow. So all summer, the leaves are busy working. They stay green while the days are long and warm.

Then fall comes. The days get shorter, and the nights get cooler. Since there is less sunlight, the tree slows down. It does not make as much food as before. It starts to get ready for winter. This is the first step in a long chain.

As the tree slows down, the green color fades away. The tree stops making new chlorophyll. The old green breaks down. As a result, other colors appear. Yellow and orange were hiding in the leaf all along. Now we can finally see them.

Some trees turn red too. Cool nights and sunny days help this happen. Sugar gets trapped inside the leaf. That sugar helps make a red color. That is why some fall days look so bright. A cool and sunny fall can make the very best reds.

Next, the tree grows a thin wall where each leaf meets its twig. This wall cuts the leaf off. Water can not get in, so the leaf dries out. It turns brown. Then a puff of wind comes along, and the leaf falls to the ground.

The fallen leaves have a job too. They rot and break down. This makes the dirt rich. Rich dirt helps the tree grow again in spring. So one fall leaf helps make the next green leaf. The chain goes around and around every year.

stops.question: What caused the tree to slow down in fall?
stops.lookFor: Shorter days mean less sun, so the tree makes less food and slows down.

stops.question: How did the green fading lead to the next thing that happened?
stops.lookFor: When the green broke down, the yellow and orange that were hiding could finally show.

stops.question: What clue word told you the leaf drying out was an effect?
stops.lookFor: The word 'so' shows the leaf dried out because the wall stopped water from getting in.

questions.q: Why do leaves turn yellow and orange in fall?
questions.a: The green breaks down, so the yellow and orange that were already there can show.

questions.q: What causes a leaf to fall off the tree?
questions.a: A thin wall cuts off water, so the leaf dries out and the wind blows it down.

questions.q: How does a fallen leaf help the tree later?
questions.a: It rots and makes the dirt rich, which helps the tree grow new leaves in spring.

sessions.title: Where Do Puddles Go?
paragraphs: After a big rain, there are puddles all over the yard, and Kai likes to jump in them. But by the next day, most of them are gone. Where did the water go? The sun is the cause. Let's find out how it works.

The sun warms the puddle, and warm water moves fast. Tiny bits of the water get so fast that they float up into the air, where we can not see them. This is called evaporation. Since the sun is out, the puddle gets a bit smaller each hour.
Wind helps too. Wind pushes the wet air away. Then dry air comes in its place. Dry air can take up more water. So on a windy day, a puddle dries up fast. On a still day, it takes much longer to go.

The water does not just go away. It rises up high in the sky. Up there, the air is cold. Cold air makes the tiny bits of water stick back together. As a result, they form small drops. Lots of drops make a cloud.

The cloud keeps getting more drops. The drops bump and join. They get big and heavy. Since they are too heavy to float, they fall. That is rain! The rain falls on the yard. It makes new puddles for Kai to jump in.

So one puddle is part of a big loop. The sun makes the water rise. Cold air makes clouds. Heavy drops make rain. Rain makes puddles. Then the sun starts it all again. This loop is called the water cycle, and it does not stop.

stops.question: What is the cause that makes the puddle get smaller?
stops.lookFor: The sun warms the water, so tiny bits of it float up into the air.

stops.question: Why does a puddle dry faster on a windy day?
stops.lookFor: Wind pushes the wet air away and brings dry air, which can take up more water.

stops.question: How did the water rising up lead to something new?
stops.lookFor: When it got high where the air is cold, the bits stuck together into drops and made a cloud.

questions.q: What causes a puddle to dry up?
questions.a: The sun warms the water and it rises into the air, and wind helps carry it away.

questions.q: Why do raindrops fall from a cloud?
questions.a: The drops join and get too heavy to float, so they fall.

questions.q: How does a dried-up puddle end up making a new puddle?
questions.a: The water rises, makes a cloud, falls as rain, and makes a new puddle.

sessions.title: Why We Sweat
paragraphs: Maya runs up and down the field in her soccer game. Soon her face gets red. Drops of sweat roll down her nose. Why does this happen? Her body is working very hard. Hard work makes heat inside her body.

Her legs burn energy from the food she ate. Burning energy makes heat. The more Maya runs, the more heat her body makes. A body that gets too hot does not work well. So it needs a way to cool off fast.

Her body has a smart trick. It sends more blood close to her skin. Then heat from the blood can escape through the skin. That is why her face looks red. The red color comes from all the extra blood near the surface of her skin.
Next, her skin makes sweat. Sweat is mostly water. It sits on her skin in tiny drops. Then the air dries them. As the sweat dries, it carries heat away with it. As a result, her skin feels cooler.

But sweating uses up water. Her body loses lots of it on a hot day. This makes her feel thirsty. Thirst is her body telling her it is time to drink. So at halftime, Maya grabs her water bottle. She drinks and drinks.

The water fills her body back up. Now it can make more sweat. More sweat helps her stay cool. Staying cool helps her play well. So one bottle of water helps her keep running hard all the way to the end of the game.

stops.question: What is causing Maya's body to change?
stops.lookFor: She is running hard, and hard work makes her body hot.

stops.question: Why does Maya's face turn red? What was the clue?
stops.lookFor: Her body sends blood near the skin to let heat out; 'that is why' signals the effect.

stops.question: How did sweating lead to the next thing that happened?
stops.lookFor: Sweating used up water, so she got thirsty and needed to drink.

questions.q: What causes Maya's body to make heat?
questions.a: Her running legs burn fuel from food, and that makes heat.

questions.q: How does sweat help Maya cool off?
questions.a: When the sweat dries on her skin, it takes heat away with it.

questions.q: Why does drinking water help Maya play well?
questions.a: Water lets her make more sweat, sweat keeps her cool, and staying cool helps her play hard.

sessions.title: What Makes Thunder
paragraphs: Have you ever seen a flash of light in a storm and then heard a loud boom? The flash is lightning, and the boom is thunder. They seem like two different things. But one is the cause of the other. Lightning is what makes thunder.

It all starts inside a storm cloud. Tiny bits of ice bump and rub as the wind tosses them around. Because of all this bumping, the cloud fills with a charge, like the spark you get from a rug. Soon the charge gets too big to hold.

Then the charge jumps. It shoots from the cloud to the ground or to another cloud. That giant spark is lightning. It is very hot. In fact, it is hotter than the top of the sun! It heats the air around it in a blink.

Hot air spreads out. Since the lightning heats the air so fast, the air does not just spread. It bursts out all at once. This push of air sends a wave through the sky. That wave is a sound wave, and we hear it as thunder.

You see the flash first and hear the boom later. That is because light moves much faster than sound. Light gets to you almost right away. Sound takes about five seconds to go one mile. So a long wait means the storm is far.

This gives people a smart safety rule. If you can hear thunder, the storm is close enough to reach you. As a result, it is time to go inside. Wait until the thunder has stopped for a while before you go back out to play.

stops.question: What caused the charge to build up in the cloud?
stops.lookFor: Bits of ice bumping and rubbing in the wind made the charge.

stops.question: How did the lightning lead to the thunder?
stops.lookFor: Lightning heated the air so fast that it burst out, sending a sound wave we hear as thunder.

stops.question: What clue words tell you why we see the flash before we hear the boom?
stops.lookFor: 'That is because' shows the cause: light moves much faster than sound.

questions.q: What causes thunder?
questions.a: Lightning heats the air so fast that it bursts outward and makes a sound wave.

questions.q: Why do we hear thunder after we see lightning?
questions.a: Light travels much faster than sound, so the sound reaches us later.

questions.q: What should you do because you hear thunder, and why?
questions.a: Go inside, because hearing thunder means the storm is close enough to reach you.

sessions.title: Why Bread Rises
paragraphs: Leo and his dad are baking bread together. They mix flour, water, salt, and a spoonful of yeast in a big bowl. At first the dough is a small, flat lump. But after an hour, it is twice as big. What made it grow? The answer is the yeast.

Yeast is a living thing that is so tiny you can not see one by itself. When yeast gets warm water and food, it wakes up. Its favorite food is sugar. The flour has some sugar in it, so the yeast starts to eat.

As the yeast eats, it makes a gas. This gas is the same kind that is in the bubbles of soda. The gas forms lots of tiny bubbles all through the dough. Since the bubbles take up space, the dough begins to puff up.

But why don't the bubbles just pop and leave? Leo's dad pushed and folded the dough for a long time. This made the dough stretchy, like a balloon. Because the dough can stretch, it traps the gas inside. That is why it rises.
Warm air matters too. Yeast works faster in a warm room. In a cold room, it works slowly. So Leo set his bowl near a sunny window. As a result, his dough rose faster than it would on a cold day.

At last the bread goes in the oven. The heat makes the bubbles grow one last time. Then the heat stops the yeast and sets the bread. The bubbles leave little holes behind. That is why each slice of bread is soft and full of holes.

stops.question: What causes the yeast to start eating?
stops.lookFor: Warm water and the sugar in the flour wake the yeast up.

stops.question: How did the yeast eating lead to the dough puffing up?
stops.lookFor: Eating made gas, the gas made bubbles, and the bubbles took up space.

stops.question: Why don't the bubbles escape? What clue word helped you?
stops.lookFor: The stretchy dough traps the gas; 'because' and 'that is why' signal the cause and effect.

questions.q: What causes the dough to rise?
questions.a: Yeast eats sugar and makes gas bubbles that get trapped in the stretchy dough.

questions.q: Why did Leo put his bowl near a sunny window?
questions.a: Yeast works faster when it is warm, so the dough would rise faster.

questions.q: Why does a slice of bread have little holes?
questions.a: The gas bubbles left holes when the oven heat set the bread.

sessions.title: Thank a Bee for Your Apple
paragraphs: Have you ever thanked a bee for your apple? You should! Without bees, many fruits would not grow. Bees do not mean to help us. They are just looking for food. But their search for food causes something big to happen.

Bees visit flowers to drink a sweet juice called nectar. To reach it, a bee crawls deep into the flower. Inside the flower is a yellow dust called pollen. As the bee moves around, the pollen sticks to its fuzzy body.

Next, the bee flies to a flower on another tree. Some of the pollen rubs off there. This is called pollination. An apple flower needs pollen from a different apple tree to make seeds. So the bee has just given the flower what it needs.

Once a flower gets the right pollen, it begins to change. Its petals fall off. The part in the middle starts to swell. It grows bigger and bigger all summer. As a result, the flower turns into an apple with seeds inside.

The seeds can grow into new apple trees one day. Those trees will make new flowers. The new flowers will make more nectar. That brings more bees. So one bee visit starts a chain that can go on for many years.

This is why farmers care so much about bees. Some farmers bring boxes of bees to their apple trees in spring. More bees means more flowers get pollen. That causes more fruit to grow. The next time you bite an apple, think of a busy bee.

stops.question: Why does pollen end up on the bee?
stops.lookFor: The bee crawls deep into the flower for nectar, and the pollen sticks to its fuzzy body.

stops.question: What happened because the flower got pollen?
stops.lookFor: The petals fell off and the middle swelled until it became an apple.

stops.question: How did one effect lead to the next in this part?
stops.lookFor: Seeds grow into trees, trees make flowers, flowers make nectar, and nectar brings more bees.

questions.q: What causes a bee to carry pollen from tree to tree?
questions.a: It is looking for nectar, and pollen sticks to it as it moves between flowers.

questions.q: What is the effect when an apple flower gets pollen from another tree?
questions.a: It can make seeds and grow into an apple.

questions.q: Why do some farmers bring boxes of bees to their trees?
questions.a: More bees means more flowers get pollen, so more fruit grows.

sessions.title: How Beavers Change a Stream
paragraphs: A beaver is a big furry animal with strong orange teeth and a flat tail. It lives in streams and ponds. Beavers are famous for building dams. When a beaver builds a dam, it changes the whole stream, and many other animals feel the effects.

Why do beavers build dams at all? They need deep water to stay safe. In deep water, a beaver can swim away from danger and hide the door to its home. So the beaver cuts down small trees with its teeth and piles up sticks, mud, and stones.

The dam blocks the moving water. Since the water can not flow past easily, it backs up behind the dam. As a result, the stream spreads out and becomes a wide, calm pond. Now the beaver has the deep water it wanted.

The new pond causes even more changes. Water spreads into the land around it and soaks the soil. Wet soil lets new plants grow, like reeds, grasses, and willows. Soon a dry area along the stream turns into a green, soggy wetland.

Those plants bring new animals. Ducks and geese nest in the reeds. Frogs lay eggs in the still water. Fish hide among the plants, and birds come to catch the fish. That is why a beaver pond is often full of life.

The dam can help people too. It slows down water after a big rain, so floods farther down the stream may be smaller. It also holds water during dry times. So one busy beaver, just trying to stay safe, can end up helping a whole valley.

stops.question: What is the cause that makes a beaver build a dam?
stops.lookFor: It needs deep water to stay safe and hide its home.

stops.question: What happened because the dam blocked the water? What clue words show it?
stops.lookFor: The water backed up and became a pond; 'since' and 'as a result' signal it.

stops.question: How did the pond lead to new animals coming?
stops.lookFor: The pond made wet soil, new plants grew, and those plants gave animals places to nest, hide, and find food.

questions.q: Why does a beaver build a dam?
questions.a: It needs deep water so it can stay safe.

questions.q: How does a beaver dam make a wetland?
questions.a: The dam makes a pond, the water soaks the soil, and new plants grow there.

questions.q: How can a beaver dam help people?
questions.a: It slows floodwater after big rains and holds water during dry times.

sessions.title: Why the Moon Changes Shape
paragraphs: Some nights the moon looks like a bright, round ball. Other nights it is a thin curve, like a fingernail. Sometimes you can not see it at all. The moon is not really changing its shape. So why does it look so different from night to night?

The first thing to know is that the moon does not make its own light, because it is just a big ball of rock. The light we see is sunlight bouncing off its surface. Because of this, only the side facing the sun is bright. The other side stays dark.

The moon also travels around Earth. One trip takes about a month. As the moon moves, we see it from a new angle each night. That is why we see a different amount of its bright side. The shapes we see are called phases.

When the moon is between Earth and the sun, its bright side faces away from us. As a result, we see almost nothing. This is called a new moon. A few nights later, the moon has moved a little, so a thin sliver of light appears.

Night after night, the bright part grows. When the moon is on the far side of Earth from the sun, we can see its whole bright face. This is a full moon. After that, the bright part shrinks again, because the moon keeps moving.

This pattern repeats over and over. People long ago watched it so closely that they used it to keep track of time. In fact, the word month comes from the word moon. So the moon's trip around Earth even helped shape our calendars.

stops.question: Why is only one side of the moon bright?
stops.lookFor: The moon makes no light of its own, so only the side facing the sun reflects sunlight.

stops.question: What causes us to see a different shape each night? What clue words helped?
stops.lookFor: The moon moves around Earth, so we see it from a new angle; 'that is why' signals the effect.

stops.question: What is the effect when the moon is between Earth and the sun?
stops.lookFor: Its bright side faces away from us, so we see almost nothing, a new moon.

questions.q: What causes the moon to seem to change shape?
questions.a: As it travels around Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit side.

questions.q: Why do we see a full moon?
questions.a: The moon is on the far side of Earth from the sun, so its whole bright face points at us.

questions.q: How did the moon's pattern affect people long ago?
questions.a: They used it to keep track of time, and the word month comes from moon.

sessions.title: Why the Ocean Is Salty
paragraphs: If you have ever swum in the ocean, you know that the water tastes salty. A lake or river usually does not. So why is the ocean so salty? The answer starts far away from the beach, on land, with rain and rocks.

Rain is not just plain water. As it falls through the air, it picks up a gas that makes it a tiny bit sour. It is a little like very weak lemon juice. Because of this, rain can slowly wear away rocks. As the rocks break down, bits of salt come loose.

Rain runs over the ground and into streams. The streams carry the tiny bits of salt along with them. Streams join to form rivers, and rivers flow to the sea. So every river is always carrying a little salt into the ocean.

River water does not taste salty. That is because there is only a small amount of salt in it. But the ocean gets salt from lots and lots of rivers. It has been collecting salt for a very, very long time. As a result, a huge amount of salt has built up.

Here is the key step. The sun warms the ocean, and water rises into the air. But the salt can not rise with it. The salt stays behind in the sea. That is why the ocean keeps its salt while the water keeps moving.

The water that rose into the air forms clouds. Then it falls as rain, and the whole chain starts again. Rain wears down rocks, rivers carry salt, and the sun leaves the salt behind. So the ocean stays salty, year after year.

stops.question: What causes the rain to wear away rocks?
stops.lookFor: Rain picks up a gas in the air that makes it a little sour, so it can slowly break down rock.

stops.question: How did the rocks breaking down lead to salt reaching the sea?
stops.lookFor: Salt came loose, streams carried it, streams joined rivers, and rivers flowed to the sea.

stops.question: What clue words tell you why the ocean keeps its salt?
stops.lookFor: 'That is why' shows the effect: water rises into the air but the salt stays behind.

questions.q: Where does the salt in the ocean first come from?
questions.a: From rocks on land that rain slowly wears away.

questions.q: Why doesn't river water taste salty?
questions.a: It only has a small amount of salt in it.

questions.q: Why does the ocean stay salty even when water rises into the air?
questions.a: The salt can not rise with the water, so it stays behind in the sea.

sessions.title: How Volcanoes Built Hawaii
paragraphs: The islands of Hawaii sit in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. They are far from any other big land. They were not always there. Each island was built by a volcano, one layer at a time. Their story is a long chain of causes and effects. It is still going on.

Deep under the ocean floor, there is a very hot spot inside the Earth. The heat there is so strong that it melts solid rock. Melted rock is lighter than the rock around it. So it slowly pushes its way up, like a bubble rising through thick syrup.

When the melted rock breaks through the ocean floor, it pours out as lava. The cold sea water cools the lava fast. It hardens into new rock. Each time the volcano erupts, the rock piles higher. At last, the pile pokes above the waves and becomes an island.

But the story does not stop there. The ocean floor is always moving, just a few inches each year. Because the floor moves and the hot spot stays put, the island is slowly carried away from the heat. As a result, its volcano is cut off and stops erupting.

But the hot spot stays put. It keeps melting rock under the new patch of ocean floor above it. That causes a brand new volcano to start growing. This is why the islands of Hawaii form a long line. The oldest ones are at one end, and the youngest are at the other.

Right now, the Big Island is the youngest, and its volcanoes still erupt. Off its coast, a new volcano is slowly growing under the water. Scientists think it may reach the top one day. That will take many thousands of years. So the chain of islands is still being built.

stops.question: Why does the melted rock move upward?
stops.lookFor: It is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it pushes its way up.

stops.question: What caused the old volcano to stop erupting? What clue words show it?
stops.lookFor: The moving ocean floor carried the island away from the hot spot; 'because' and 'as a result' signal it.

stops.question: How did one island moving away lead to a new island?
stops.lookFor: The hot spot was then under new ocean floor, so it started building a new volcano there.

questions.q: What causes a Hawaiian island to form?
questions.a: Melted rock from a hot spot pours out as lava, hardens, and piles up until it rises above the water.

questions.q: Why do the Hawaiian islands form a long line?
questions.a: The ocean floor keeps moving over the hot spot, so new volcanoes form one after another.

questions.q: What is the effect of an island moving away from the hot spot?
questions.a: Its volcano is cut off from the melted rock and stops erupting.

sessions.title: Why a Guitar Makes Music
paragraphs: When Amara plucks a string on her guitar, a clear note rings out across the room. It seems almost like magic. But there is a simple reason the guitar makes sound. Every note begins with a movement so fast that our eyes can barely see it.

When Amara pulls the string and lets go, it starts to shake back and forth very quickly. This shaking is called vibration. A string can shake hundreds of times every second. Because the string moves so fast, it looks a little blurry while the note is playing.

The moving string pushes on the air around it. Each push squeezes the air a little, and then the air spreads back out. This causes a wave to travel through the air, much like a ripple moving across a pond. That wave of squeezed air is a sound wave.

When the sound wave reaches Amara's ears, it makes her eardrums shake too. Her ears then send a message to her brain. As a result, she hears the note. So the sound she hears is really the string's shaking, passed from the string to the air to her ears.

A string all by itself is quiet, since it only pushes a small amount of air. That is why a guitar has a hollow wooden body. The shaking travels from the string into the wood. Then the wood shakes the air inside the body, and the sound gets much louder.

Amara can also change the note. A thin, tight string shakes faster, so it makes a higher sound. A thick, loose string shakes slower, so its sound is lower. When she presses a string with her finger, she makes it shorter. That makes it shake faster and play higher.

stops.question: What caused the string to start vibrating?
stops.lookFor: Amara pulled the string and let it go, so it shook back and forth.

stops.question: How did the string's shaking lead to Amara hearing a note?
stops.lookFor: The string pushed the air, the air carried a sound wave, the wave shook her eardrums, and her brain heard it.

stops.question: What clue words explain why the guitar has a hollow body?
stops.lookFor: 'Since' and 'that is why' show that a string alone is quiet, so the hollow body makes it louder.

questions.q: What causes a guitar string to make sound?
questions.a: Its vibration pushes the air and makes a sound wave.

questions.q: What is the effect of the guitar's hollow wooden body?
questions.a: The wood shakes the air inside, which makes the sound much louder.

questions.q: Why does pressing a string make a higher note?
questions.a: It makes the string shorter, so it vibrates faster.

sessions.title: Why Ice Floats
paragraphs: Most things shrink a little when they freeze. Water is different. When water turns into ice, it actually spreads out and takes up more space. This one strange fact causes a chain of effects that helps fish and frogs make it through the long, cold winter.

As water cools down and freezes, its tiny parts line up in a neat pattern with lots of open space. Because of all that space, ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water. That is why an ice cube floats at the top of your glass instead of sinking.

The same thing happens in a pond. When winter comes, the air above the pond gets very cold. The water at the top cools first and turns into ice. Since the ice is lighter than the water, it stays on the surface and forms a solid lid over the pond.

That icy lid works like a blanket. It blocks the cold wind from touching the water below. As a result, the water under the ice stays cold but does not freeze solid. Deep in the pond, the water stays a little above freezing all winter long.

This is very good news for the animals living there. Fish keep swimming slowly in the deeper water. Some frogs and turtles rest in the mud at the bottom. Because the water below the ice stays liquid, they can stay safe through the coldest months.

Think about what would happen if ice sank instead. Each new layer of ice would drop to the bottom, and the pond would freeze from the bottom up. The whole pond could turn solid. So the simple fact that ice floats helps keep winter ponds full of life.

stops.question: What causes ice to be lighter than liquid water?
stops.lookFor: When water freezes, its tiny parts line up with lots of open space.

stops.question: How did the ice lid lead to the water below staying liquid?
stops.lookFor: The ice blocks the cold wind like a blanket, so the water under it does not freeze solid.

stops.question: What clue word tells you why the fish and frogs stay safe?
stops.lookFor: 'Because' shows the cause: the water below the ice stays liquid.

questions.q: Why does an ice cube float?
questions.a: Ice has open space inside, so it is lighter than the same amount of water.

questions.q: What is the effect of ice forming on top of a pond?
questions.a: It acts like a blanket so the water underneath does not freeze solid.

questions.q: What might happen if ice sank instead of floating?
questions.a: The pond could freeze from the bottom up and turn solid.

sessions.title: How a Hot Air Balloon Flies
paragraphs: Early on a calm morning, a giant striped balloon lifts quietly into the sky, carrying a basket full of people. There is no engine and no propeller. So what pushes it upward? The answer is heat, and it starts a chain of causes and effects that lets the balloon fly.

Inside the basket, the pilot controls a burner that shoots a tall flame up into the open bottom of the balloon. The flame heats the air trapped inside. Because air spreads out when it gets warm, some of it is pushed out. The air left inside becomes thinner.

Thin, warm air is lighter than the same amount of cool air. Now the air inside the balloon is lighter than the cooler air all around it. As a result, the cool air pushes up from below, the same way water pushes a beach ball to the top of a pool.

Once the balloon is lighter than the air around it, it begins to rise. The pilot adds more bursts of heat to climb higher. When the pilot stops using the burner, the air inside slowly cools. Cooler air is heavier, so the balloon drifts back down.

A balloon has no steering wheel, so how does a pilot choose where to go? The wind often blows in different directions at different heights. That is why a pilot moves the balloon up or down to find a breeze going the right way. Changing height is a clever way to steer.

This is also why balloon rides often happen at sunrise. In the early morning, the air is usually calm and the winds are gentle. Later in the day, the sun warms the ground, which stirs up gusty winds. So the same heat that lifts the balloon can also make flying harder.

stops.question: What happens to the air because the burner heats it?
stops.lookFor: It spreads out, some is pushed out, and the air left inside becomes thinner.

stops.question: How did the air getting thinner lead to the next step?
stops.lookFor: The thin air is lighter than the cool air outside, so the cool air pushes the balloon up.

stops.question: What clue words tell you why a pilot moves up or down?
stops.lookFor: 'That is why' shows the cause: winds blow different ways at different heights.

questions.q: What causes a hot air balloon to rise?
questions.a: Heated air inside is lighter than the cooler air around it, so the balloon is pushed up.

questions.q: What is the effect when the pilot stops using the burner?
questions.a: The air inside cools and gets heavier, so the balloon drifts down.

questions.q: Why do balloon rides often happen at sunrise?
questions.a: The air is calm early, but later the sun warms the ground and stirs up gusty winds.

sessions.title: Why Popcorn Pops
paragraphs: When you heat a handful of hard, tiny corn kernels, something amazing happens. One by one, they burst into fluffy white puffs that are much bigger than before. Popcorn seems like a magic trick, but every pop is caused by a hidden drop of water inside each kernel.

A popcorn kernel has three main parts. On the outside is a hard, shiny shell called the hull. Inside is a soft, starchy center, and mixed into that center is a small amount of water. The hull is special because it is very strong and does not let water out easily.

When the kernel is heated in a pan, the water inside gets hotter and hotter. At last, the water turns into steam. Steam takes up much more space than water, so it pushes outward. Since the strong hull keeps the steam trapped inside, the pressure keeps building.

At the same time, the heat changes the starch inside the kernel. It turns soft and gooey, like a thick paste. Finally, the pressure becomes too much for the hull to hold back. The shell bursts open with a pop, and the steam rushes out all at once.

As the steam escapes, it puffs the gooey starch outward into a foam. The cool air quickly hardens the foam into a crunchy shape. This is why a popped kernel is so light and full of tiny holes. It is mostly starch and air, held together like a frozen cloud.

Sometimes a few kernels never pop. They stay hard at the bottom of the bowl. This often happens because the hull had a tiny crack, or the kernel had dried out too much. Either way, the steam leaked out slowly instead of building up. So it never had enough push to burst.

stops.question: Why is the hull important? What clue word helped you?
stops.lookFor: It is strong and does not let water escape; the word 'because' gives the reason.

stops.question: How did the water heating up lead to pressure building?
stops.lookFor: The water turned to steam, the steam took up more space, and the hull kept it trapped.

stops.question: What caused the popped kernel to be light and full of holes?
stops.lookFor: Escaping steam puffed the soft starch into a foam that hardened in the air.

questions.q: What causes a popcorn kernel to pop?
questions.a: Water inside turns to steam, the pressure builds, and the hull bursts open.

questions.q: What is the effect of the steam rushing out?
questions.a: It puffs the soft starch into a foam that hardens into a crunchy shape.

questions.q: Why do some kernels never pop?

sessions.title: Why We Have Seasons
paragraphs: In many places, summer brings long, hot days, and winter brings short, chilly ones. Many people guess that summer happens because Earth moves closer to the sun. That idea makes sense, but it is not correct. The real cause of the seasons is the way Earth is tilted.

Earth spins around an imaginary line called its axis, which runs from the North Pole to the South Pole. This line is not straight up and down. Instead, it leans to one side, a little like a spinning top that is tipping. Earth keeps this same lean all year long.

Because of the tilt, the northern half of Earth leans toward the sun during part of the year. When this happens, sunlight hits that half more directly, and the sun climbs higher in the sky. Direct sunlight is stronger, so the ground and air heat up. That is summer in the north.

Leaning toward the sun also makes the days longer. The sun rises earlier and sets later, which gives the land more hours to soak up warmth. As a result, each day adds a little more heat than the night can take away, and the weather keeps getting warmer.

Six months later, Earth has moved to the other side of the sun. Now the northern half leans away. The sunlight comes in at a low slant and spreads out over a wider area, so it feels weaker. The days are also shorter. That is why the north has winter.

Here is the most surprising effect. When it is summer in the northern half of Earth, it is winter in the southern half, because the two halves lean in opposite ways. So while children in Canada build snowmen in December, children in Australia might be splashing at the beach.

sessions.title: Why Coral Turns White
paragraphs: A coral reef looks like a bright underwater garden, but the corals that build it are really animals. Each coral is made of tiny creatures called polyps. Most of their color comes from partners living inside them. When the ocean gets too warm, that teamwork can break apart.

Inside a coral live millions of tiny algae, which are a lot like plants. The algae use sunlight to make food and share much of it with the coral. In return, the coral gives them a safe home. Because the algae are colorful, they give the coral its brown, green, or gold shades.

This teamwork goes well as long as the water is not too hot. But when the ocean stays too warm for several weeks, the algae become stressed. They start to make things that can harm the coral. As a result, the coral pushes the algae out of its body to protect itself.

Without the algae, the coral loses its color. Its clear body lets the white skeleton underneath show through, so the coral looks pale or bright white. This is called coral bleaching. A bleached coral is still alive, but it has lost the partner that gave it most of its food.

Since the coral is no longer getting enough food, it grows weak and slow. If the water stays warm for too long, the coral may not get better. That hurts the whole reef, because many fish and crabs need healthy coral for shelter and food.

There is good news. If the water cools down soon enough, the algae can move back in, and the coral can get its color back. That is why scientists keep a close eye on how warm the ocean gets. Caring for reefs today helps them stay bright in the future.

sessions.title: How Water Carved the Grand Canyon
paragraphs: The Grand Canyon in Arizona is so huge that it can take hours to drive from one rim to the other, even though they look close. This giant gap in the Earth was not made all at once. It was carved slowly by water, through a long chain of causes and effects.

The main cause is the Colorado River, which flows along the canyon floor. Moving water carries sand, pebbles, and even boulders along with it. As these pieces tumble downstream, they scrape the riverbed like sandpaper. Over millions of years, it cut the canyon deeper.

Something else made the river cut faster. Over a very long time, the land in this area was slowly pushed upward. Because the land rose, the river ran downhill more steeply, so its water moved faster and had more power. Faster water could carry bigger rocks that scraped even harder.

The river explains the depth, but the canyon is also very wide. Rain, ice, and wind make the walls crumble. When water seeps into cracks and freezes, it grows and pries the rock apart. As a result, chunks break loose and fall to the river, which carries them away.

Not every layer of rock wears away at the same speed. Hard layers stand up to the water and form steep cliffs, while soft layers crumble more easily and form gentle slopes. That is why the canyon walls look like a giant staircase, with colorful stripes stacked on top of each other.

The carving has not stopped. Each flood or storm changes the canyon a tiny bit. They are far too slow to notice in one day. Still, each grain of sand the river carries away is part of the same slow work that made the canyon.

stops.lookFor: Sand, pebbles, and boulders carried by the water scraped the riverbed like sandpaper.

stops.lookFor: Rising land made the river steeper, so the water moved faster, carried bigger rocks, and scraped harder.

questions.a: The Colorado River and the rocks it carries slowly wore away the rock.

questions.a: Rain, ice, and wind crumble the walls, and freezing water pries rock apart.

questions.q: Why do some layers form cliffs and others form slopes?

sessions.title: What Space Does to Astronauts
paragraphs: On Earth, your body is always working against gravity, even when you stand still. Gravity pulls you down, so your muscles and bones must stay strong to hold you up. In space, that steady pull no longer holds astronauts down, and their bodies begin to change.

On the space station, astronauts float instead of walk. Moving across the station takes only a gentle push. Because their legs and backs no longer carry their weight, those muscles get far less work than usual. As a result, the muscles slowly start to shrink and grow weak.

Bones change as well. On Earth, walking and jumping send a signal that tells the body to keep bones thick and strong. In space, that signal grows quiet. The body takes away bone faster than it can build it back, so the bones slowly get thinner, mostly in the hips and legs.

Floating also changes how fluids like blood move. Without gravity pulling them down, they shift up toward the head and chest. That is why astronauts often have puffy faces and stuffy noses in their first days in space. Some even notice small changes in how well they see.

To fight these effects, astronauts exercise for about two hours almost every day. They run on a treadmill while stretchy straps hold them down, and they lift against a machine that pushes back. Since this gives muscles and bones the work they need, it helps keep them strong.

When astronauts come back to Earth, gravity suddenly feels heavy again. Their muscles need time to adjust, so walking feels wobbly for a while. With rest and practice, their bodies usually recover in a few weeks or months. Studying these changes helps doctors keep people healthy on Earth, too.

questions.a: Without the stress of walking and jumping, the body removes bone material faster than it rebuilds it.

sessions.title: Pip Digs Holes
paragraphs: Rosa had a new dog named Pip, and he was small and brown. Pip was a good dog, but he had one big problem. He dug holes all over the yard. He dug by the fence and by the back steps. One day he even dug in Mom's bean patch! Mom was not happy, because her beans fell over in the dirt.

First, Rosa tried to yell at Pip to make him stop. Pip stopped for a bit, but when Rosa went in, he dug again. Then she tried to fill the holes with rocks. That did not work, because Pip just dug a new hole next to the old one. Now the yard had holes and rocks.

Rosa sat on the steps and felt sad. She watched Pip for a long time to see what he did. She saw that he dug when he was alone with no one to play with. Pip was not bad at all. He was bored! He had lots of pep and no job to do.

So Rosa decided to give Pip a job of his own. She and Dad made a dig box in the back of the yard and filled it with soft sand. Rosa hid a ball and a bone deep in the sand. Then she showed Pip the box. He sniffed and dug until he found the bone! His tail went wild.

Each day, Rosa hid new toys in the box for Pip to find. She took him on a long walk each day, too. Pip was tired and glad, and he dug only in his box. Mom's beans grew tall again. Finally, the problem was solved. Rosa learned that if you find out why a problem happens, you can fix it.

stops.lookFor: Pip digs holes all over the yard, even in Mom's beans.

questions.a: He was bored and alone with lots of energy and nothing to do.

sessions.title: The Kite Tail
paragraphs: Kai got a red kite with a long string for his birthday. He took it to the park with Grandpa on a day when the wind was strong. Kai held the string tight and ran. But the kite did not go up. It spun in a circle and then hit the grass. That was the problem.

First, Kai tried to run as fast as he could. The kite went up a bit, and then it fell down hard. Next, he tried to toss it high up in the air. The kite flipped and fell right on his head. Kai did not laugh, because he was mad.

Grandpa sat down on the grass with Kai and said, "Let's look at it." They looked at the kite and then at the tail. Grandpa held the kite up, and it tipped to one side. The tail was too short! A short tail can not hold a kite still in the wind.

Kai decided to make the tail long. He had a long ribbon in his bag from his gift, and Grandpa helped him tie it on. Now the tail was twice as long. Kai held the kite up and let the wind take it. He did not run this time. He just let out the string bit by bit.

Up, up, up went the kite! It did not spin, and it did not fall. It flew high over the tall trees. Finally, the problem was solved, and Kai smiled at Grandpa. He learned that trying hard is not always the answer. Sometimes you need to stop and look at what is wrong.

stops.lookFor: His kite will not fly; it spins and falls even though the wind is strong.

stops.question: Why didn't running fast or tossing the kite fix the problem?
stops.lookFor: Something was wrong with the kite itself, so trying harder did not help.

stops.lookFor: Yes, because a longer tail can keep the kite steady, which was the real problem.

questions.a: Running faster and tossing the kite into the air.

questions.q: What did Kai and Grandpa find out was wrong?
questions.a: The kite's tail was too short to keep it steady.

questions.q: What lesson did Kai learn?
questions.a: Trying harder is not always the answer; sometimes you need to stop and look at what is wrong.

sessions.title: The Ball and the Creek
paragraphs: Nia and her friends played soccer each day in a big field by a creek. They had a lot of fun, but there was a problem. The field sloped down to the creek. When a kid kicked hard, the ball rolled all the way down the hill. Splash! It went in the creek and then floated away from them.

First, the kids tried to kick the ball soft. That did not work, since soft kicks are no fun and the ball still rolled. Next, they tried to put Omar by the creek so he could stop the ball. But Omar got bored, because he wanted to play too. And the ball still got right past him.

The kids sat down in the grass to think about it. Nia looked at the hill and then at the creek. Then she saw a pile of old logs by the path. "What if we make a wall?" she asked. A wall would stop the ball before it got to the water, and her friends liked the plan a lot.

They decided to ask Ben, the park helper, if they could use the logs. He said yes, so the kids rolled the logs to the foot of the hill. Ben helped them line the logs up in a long row. It was hard work, and they all got muddy. But they did it together.

The next day, Jayden kicked the ball hard, and it flew past the goal. It rolled down the hill and hit the logs with a bump. Then it stopped, and there was no splash! The kids cheered. Finally, the problem was solved. Now Omar could play, and the ball stayed dry. Nia was proud of her team.

sessions.title: Sticky Pancakes
paragraphs: On Saturday mornings, Amara and her dad made pancakes. This week, Amara wanted to cook them all by herself. She mixed the flour, eggs, and milk in a big bowl. She poured some of the mix into the pan. But when she tried to flip the pancake, it stuck. It tore into messy bits.

Amara had a problem. First, she tried to flip the next pancake faster. It still stuck to the pan. Then she tried a bigger spatula. The pancake folded in half and ripped down the middle. Now she had a plate of broken pancakes. She felt like giving up.

Her dad came into the kitchen and looked at the pan. He asked her what she had done. Amara told him each step. Dad nodded and smiled. "You forgot two things," he said. The pan was not hot enough, and it had no butter. Pancakes need both to cook right.

Amara decided to try again the right way. She put a little butter in the pan. She waited until it sizzled. Then she poured a small circle of the mix. She watched for tiny bubbles to pop on top. That meant it was time to flip.

She slid the spatula under the pancake and flipped it. It landed with a soft plop! It was round and golden brown. Finally, Amara had solved her problem. She made a whole stack of good pancakes. She learned that cooking is like science. Each step counts, and if you skip one, it can change the whole thing.

sessions.title: Drum Practice
paragraphs: Malik loved his new drum. He wanted to play in the school band in the spring. He needed to practice every day after school. But there was a big problem. His baby sister, Lila, took a nap at the same time. Each time Malik hit the drum, Lila woke up and cried.

First, Malik tried to play very softly. He tapped the drum with just the tips of his sticks. Lila still woke up. Then he tried to practice in the garage. But the garage was cold and dark, and the sound still came through the wall. Lila cried even louder.

Malik felt stuck. If he did not practice, he would not get better. If he did practice, his sister could not sleep. He sat on the stairs and thought about it. Then he had an idea. Maybe the problem was not the drum. Maybe it was the time.

Malik decided to talk to his mom. Together they looked at Lila's nap schedule. She always slept from three to four. She was awake and happy after that. So Malik could practice at four thirty, after her nap. Mom said that plan made a lot of sense.

The next day, Malik did his homework first while Lila slept. Then, at four thirty, he played his drum. Lila sat in her chair and clapped her hands. She liked the music! Finally, the problem was solved. Malik practiced every day, and Lila got her nap. Now she is his biggest fan.

stops.lookFor: The problem might be when he practices, not the drum itself.

questions.a: He changed his practice time to after Lila's nap.

sessions.title: The Cardboard Rocket
paragraphs: Theo and his friend Zoe wanted to build a rocket. It was not a real one, but a tall cardboard rocket for their space project at school. They stacked three big boxes on top of each other. They painted them silver. They added a pointy paper top. But the rocket had a problem. It kept falling over.

First, they tried taping the boxes together with lots of tape. The rocket stood for a minute. Then it tipped and crashed onto the rug. Next, they tried leaning it against the wall. That worked until someone walked by. Then it slid sideways and fell again.

Zoe looked closely at the rocket. The top box was the biggest one. The bottom box was the smallest. "It's upside down!" she said. Heavy things on top make a tower tip over. Real rockets are wide and heavy at the bottom. That keeps them steady.

They decided to build it again. This time, they put the biggest box on the bottom. The middle box went next. The smallest box went on top. Theo put some books inside the bottom box to make it heavy. Then they taped three cardboard fins around the base.

They stepped back and held their breath. The rocket stood tall and straight. Theo gave it a small push. It wobbled, but it did not fall. Finally, their problem was solved! At school, their rocket stood in the hall all week. They learned that a strong base holds everything up.

stops.lookFor: The biggest, heaviest box was on top; flipping the order would make the rocket steady.

questions.a: The biggest box was on top, so the rocket was top-heavy.

sessions.title: The Cloudy Fish Tank
paragraphs: Imani's class had a fish tank in the back of the room with three goldfish in it. Each week, one student got to be the fish helper. This week it was Imani's turn. But on Monday, she noticed a problem. The water in the tank was cloudy and green, and she could barely see the fish.

First, Imani tried to fix it by giving the fish more food. She thought maybe they were hungry. But the next morning, the water looked even worse. Then she tried adding fresh water from the sink to the top of the tank. That did not help either. The water stayed cloudy and green.

Imani decided to ask her teacher, Miss Hana, for help. Together they looked up fish care in a library book. They learned that extra food is bad for a tank. Fish only eat a little, and the rest sinks and rots. That makes the water dirty. They also learned that sunlight helps green slime grow, and the tank was next to a sunny window.

Now Imani understood what was really wrong. She had made the problem worse by adding food! So she and Miss Hana made a new plan. They would feed the fish only a small pinch once a day. They would clean part of the water each week. They also moved the tank away from the window.

It took about a week, but the water slowly turned clear again. The goldfish swam happily around their little castle. Finally, the problem was solved. Imani made a chart so every fish helper would know the rules. She learned that a quick fix can sometimes make things worse. It helps to find the real cause first.

sessions.title: The Bridge of Blocks
paragraphs: Omar loved playing a building game where he could explore a world made of blocks. One day, he found a wide blue river in the game. On the other side, he could see a tall tower full of treasure. He really wanted to reach it. But there was one problem. His player could not swim that far.

First, Omar tried jumping across the river from a big hill. His player landed in the middle of the water and floated back to shore. Next, he tried building a tall stack of blocks to climb over. But the stack only went up, and it did not reach the other side. Omar groaned.

His older sister, Sofia, sat down to watch. She asked him what blocks he had in his bag. Omar showed her. He had wood, stone, and a few boards. Sofia pointed out that he kept building up, but the river was wide, not tall. He did not need to go higher. He needed to go across.

Omar decided to build a bridge. He placed one wood block at the edge of the water. Then he stepped onto it and placed another one in front of it. Block by block, the bridge grew longer. When he ran out of wood, he used stone. It took a while, but he kept going.

At last, the bridge touched the other side of the river. Omar's player walked across and climbed up the tower. Inside, he found a chest full of shiny gems. Finally, his problem was solved! Omar thanked Sofia for her help. He learned that the first idea is not always right. Thinking about the shape of a problem can lead to the answer.

sessions.title: The Foggy Crosswalk
paragraphs: Every morning, a crossing guard named Miss Ava helped kids cross the busy street by Leo's school. She held up a bright red stop sign so the cars would stop. But in the fall, the mornings got foggy. Drivers had a hard time seeing her. One day, a car stopped very late. Leo knew this was a problem.

Leo told his friend Marcus, and they decided to help. First, they tried calling out to the cars to slow down. But drivers could not hear them with their windows up. Next, they tried waving their arms at the corner. That did not work either. In the thick gray fog, the boys were as hard to see as Miss Ava.

Leo thought about it on the walk home. What do people use to be seen in the dark? He remembered his bike helmet. It had a small strip on the back that shined when car lights hit it. That kind of strip is called a reflector. It bounces light back toward the driver.

Leo and Marcus decided to share their idea with the principal. She loved it and called the city. A week later, Miss Ava got a new vest with shiny stripes. Her stop sign got a blinking light on top. The city also put up a yellow sign that said School Crossing Ahead.

On the next foggy morning, Leo watched from the corner. The car lights hit Miss Ava's vest, and it glowed bright. Every car slowed down early. Finally, the problem was solved. Miss Ava gave Leo and Marcus a big thumbs up. They learned that kids can help their community by speaking up with a good idea.

stops.lookFor: In the fog, drivers cannot see Miss Ava well, so cars stop too late.

sessions.title: The Wobbly Dinosaur
paragraphs: Eli had saved his money for months to buy a wooden dinosaur skeleton kit. It was a long-necked dinosaur, the kind that ate leaves from the tops of tall trees. He spent all Saturday morning fitting the pieces together. When he was done, it looked great. But as soon as he let go, the whole dinosaur tipped forward onto its nose.

Eli had a problem, and he was not going to give up. First, he tried pushing the legs deeper into the base so they would grip tighter. The dinosaur stood for a few seconds, then leaned and fell again. Next, he tried propping up the head with a stack of books. That kept it standing, but it looked silly.

Eli decided to learn more about how real dinosaurs stood. He found a library book about dinosaur bones in museums. He learned that long-necked dinosaurs also had long, heavy tails. The tail helped balance the weight of the neck, like two kids on a seesaw. Then Eli looked at his model and gasped. He had forgotten to put on the tail!

The tail pieces were still in the box, hidden under the paper with the steps. Eli snapped them together with care, one bone at a time. Then he attached the tail to the back of the hips. Now the model stretched almost the whole length of the table. He held his breath and slowly let go.

This time, the dinosaur stayed still. The long tail balanced the long neck, just like the book said. Finally, his problem was solved. Eli put the model on his shelf for all to see. He learned that when something does not work, it helps to study how it works in real life. Sometimes the answer is a missing piece.

questions.a: Pushing the legs deeper into the base and propping the head up with books.

questions.a: It had no tail to balance the weight of its long neck.

questions.a: When something does not work, study how it works in real life; sometimes the answer is a missing piece.

sessions.title: The Sandcastle and the Tide
paragraphs: Ava and her brother Jordan spent their first beach day building the biggest sandcastle they had ever made. It had four towers, a tall wall, and a deep moat around the outside. They worked on it all morning by the water. But after lunch, the waves started to creep closer. Soon a big wave rushed in and knocked down a tower.

The kids had a problem, and they wanted to save their castle. First, they tried building the wall higher to block the water. The next wave pushed right through it. Then they tried digging the moat deeper so the water would fill it instead. That worked for a few minutes. But the moat filled up fast and spilled into the castle.

Their grandmother was sitting under the umbrella, and she called them over. She explained that the ocean has tides. About twice a day, the water slowly comes up the beach, and then it slowly goes back out. In the afternoon, the tide was coming in. No wall made of sand could stop the whole ocean from rising.

Ava and Jordan looked at each other and decided to try a new plan. Instead of fighting the water, they would move away from it. The next morning, they picked a spot farther up the beach, near a line of dried seaweed. Grandma told them that line showed how high the water usually came.

They built a bigger castle in the new spot. They wet the sand with buckets so it would stay firm. That afternoon, the tide came in again, but the waves stopped a few steps away from the moat. Finally, the problem was solved, and their castle stood tall all day. They learned that some problems cannot be fought, but you can plan around them.

stops.question: What is the problem in the story?
stops.lookFor: The waves are coming closer and knocking down their sandcastle.

stops.question: Why didn't a higher wall or a deeper moat save the castle?
stops.lookFor: The water was too strong; it pushed through the wall and overflowed the moat.

stops.question: What did Grandma explain, and how does it change what the kids should do?
stops.lookFor: The tide comes in every afternoon and cannot be stopped, so they need to build somewhere the water will not reach.

questions.q: What were the two tries that failed?
questions.a: Building the wall higher and digging the moat deeper.

questions.q: Why could the kids not stop the water?
questions.a: The tide was coming in, and no sand wall can stop the ocean from rising.

questions.q: How did they finally solve the problem?
questions.a: They built the castle farther up the beach, above the seaweed line where the water usually reached.

sessions.title: Lost in the Sun
paragraphs: Maya played center field for her baseball team, the Hornets. She was fast and had a strong arm. But this season, she had a problem she could not explain. Every time a high fly ball came toward her in an afternoon game, she lost sight of it. The ball would vanish into the bright sky and drop on the grass beside her.

First, Maya tried to fix it by practicing more. She asked her dad to hit her fly balls every evening after dinner. She caught almost all of them, which made her even more confused. Then she tried standing farther back in the outfield. But that only meant that short hits dropped in front of her. In the next game, she missed two more balls.

After the game, Coach Ben asked her when the misses happened. Maya thought hard. Her practice with Dad was in the evening, when the sun was low behind the houses. But the games were in the afternoon, and center field faced right toward the sun. The problem was not her catching at all. It was the bright light in her eyes.

Maya decided to try two things that real outfielders use. First, she borrowed a pair of sunglasses made for sports. Next, her coach showed her how to hold up her glove to block the sun while she watched the ball. They practiced in the afternoon so the light would be the same as in a game.

At the next game, a batter hit a high fly ball right toward center field. Maya lifted her glove to shade her eyes and kept watching. The ball dropped right into her mitt, and her team cheered. Finally, the problem was solved. Maya learned that practice only helps when it matches the real problem you are facing.

stops.question: What problem is Maya having?
stops.lookFor: She loses high fly balls in the sky during afternoon games and they drop next to her.

stops.question: Why do you think catching well at evening practice did not fix her problem?
stops.lookFor: Evening practice was different from the games; something about the games caused the misses.

stops.lookFor: In afternoon games, she faces the sun, so the bright light hides the ball.

questions.a: Practicing fly balls with her dad in the evening and standing farther back in the outfield.

questions.a: The sun was low and behind the houses then, so it was not in her eyes like during games.

questions.q: How did Maya solve the problem?
questions.a: She wore sports sunglasses and learned to block the sun with her glove, practicing in afternoon light.

sessions.title: The Muddy Garden Path
paragraphs: Mateo and his grandmother had a small plot in the community garden at the end of their street. They grew tomatoes, peppers, and sunflowers there. To reach it, they walked down a long dirt path. That spring brought more rain than usual, and the path turned into a muddy stream after every storm.

The gardeners agreed that they had a problem, so they tried a few quick fixes. First, they laid wooden boards across the worst puddles. But the boards sank into the soft mud and got slippery. Next, someone dumped a pile of extra dirt on the path to raise it up. When the next storm came, the dirt washed away and made the mud even deeper.

Mateo wondered where all the water was coming from. During the next storm, he put on his raincoat and went out to watch. He saw that the path was the lowest part of the garden. Rain from every plot ran downhill and collected there with nowhere to go. Mateo realized they had been fixing the path when they should have been fixing the water.

He shared what he saw at the next garden meeting, and the group decided to try a new plan. Together they dug a shallow ditch along one side of the path. They filled it with gravel so water could flow toward a grassy field. They also set rain barrels under the shed roof to save water for dry weeks.

When the next big storm came, Mateo ran out to check. The rain trickled into the ditch and drained away, and the barrels filled to the top. Finally, the problem was solved, and the gardeners came back with clean shoes. Mateo learned that watching a problem closely can show you its real cause.

stops.question: What is the problem in the community garden?
stops.lookFor: Heavy rain turns the path into a muddy stream, making it hard to reach the plots.

stops.question: Why did the boards and extra dirt fail?
stops.lookFor: They covered up the mud but did not deal with where the water was coming from, so the boards sank and the dirt washed away.

stops.question: What did Mateo discover by watching the storm, and why does it matter?
stops.lookFor: The path was the lowest spot, so all the rain collected there; they needed to move the water, not just fix the path.
