placement.title: The Red Kite
paragraphs: Nia has a red kite. It has a long yellow tail. She takes it to the park with her daddy. The wind is very strong today. Nia runs fast across the grass. The kite goes up and up. Soon it is flying over the tallest trees.

Then the wind stops. The kite falls down. It lands in a tall tree. Nia is upset. She can not reach it. Her daddy can not reach it either. A helper from the park walks over with a long pole. He hooks the string with the pole. Slowly, he pulls the kite down. Nia gives him a happy smile.

Later the wind comes back. This time Nia holds the string tightly. She keeps her kite away from the trees. It flies for a long, long time. At home, Nia puts the kite on her bedroom wall. She wants to fly it again next Saturday.

questions.q: What color is Nia's kite?
questions.a: Red.

questions.q: Where does the kite land when the wind stops?
questions.a: In a tall tree.

questions.q: The park helper walks over "with a long pole" and uses it to reach the kite. What is a "pole"?
questions.a: A long stick.

questions.q: Why does Nia keep her kite away from the trees at the end?
questions.a: So it will not get stuck in a tree again.

questions.q: The story has a problem and a fix. What is the problem, and how is it fixed?
questions.a: The kite gets stuck in a tree; a park helper pulls it down with a pole.

placement.title: From Egg to Frog
paragraphs: A frog starts life as a tiny egg. A mother frog lays lots of eggs in a pond. The eggs are soft, like jelly. They float together in the water. Each egg has a little black dot inside. The dot is a baby frog.

Soon the eggs hatch. Out come tadpoles. A tadpole looks like a little fish. It has a long tail to swim with. It has no legs yet. It lives under the water and eats tiny plants. It breathes with gills, the same as a fish.

Then the tadpole begins to change. First it grows back legs. Next it grows front legs. Its tail gets smaller and smaller. It grows lungs, so it can breathe air. At last it hops out of the pond. Now it is a frog! One day it may lay eggs too.

questions.q: Where does a mother frog lay her eggs?
questions.a: In a pond (in the water).

questions.q: What does a tadpole use to swim?
questions.a: Its long tail.

questions.q: The eggs "hatch" and "out come tadpoles." What does "hatch" mean?
questions.a: To break open so the baby comes out.

questions.q: Why can a tadpole not live on land like a frog?
questions.a: It breathes with gills, not lungs, and has no legs yet.

questions.q: How is this passage put in order?
questions.a: In time order, the steps from egg to tadpole to frog.

placement.title: Bath Day for Biscuit
paragraphs: Biscuit is a big brown dog. He loves to roll in mud. Today he is very dirty. Leo says, "It is bath day, Biscuit!" Biscuit hears the word bath. He runs under the table. He does not want to come out.

Leo has a plan. He gets a treat from the jar. He holds it out low. Biscuit sniffs and creeps out. Leo leads him to the tub. He fills it with warm water. He adds soap that smells like apples. Biscuit gets wet and sudsy. He looks very silly. Leo laughs and laughs.

Then Biscuit shakes. Water flies all over the room! Now Leo is wet too. Mom comes in with two big towels. One is for Biscuit. One is for Leo. Biscuit is clean and soft now. He curls up by Leo for a nap.

questions.q: What does Biscuit love to roll in?
questions.a: Mud.

questions.q: What does the soap smell like?
questions.a: Apples.

questions.q: Biscuit "sniffs and creeps out" from under the table. What does "creeps" mean?
questions.a: Moves slowly and quietly.

questions.q: Why does Biscuit hide under the table?
questions.a: He does not want a bath.

questions.q: Why does the author tell us that Leo gets a treat from the jar?
questions.a: It shows how Leo gets Biscuit to come out from under the table.

placement.title: Amara in the Goal
paragraphs: Amara played on a soccer team called the Comets. Most days she played on defense. But today the goalie was sick at home. Coach Ben looked at Amara. "Can you play in the goal today?" he asked. Amara felt her stomach flip. She had never done it before.

She put on the big goalie gloves. They felt strange and puffy on her hands. The other team kicked the ball hard. Amara jumped to the left and missed. The ball went in. Her cheeks felt hot. Her friend Kai ran over. "Keep your eyes on the ball," he said. "You can do this."

Amara took a deep breath. The next time, she watched the ball closely. She dove and caught it with both hands! Her team cheered loudly. The Comets won the game by one goal. After the game, Coach Ben gave Amara a high five. She smiled all the way home.

questions.q: What was the name of Amara's team?
questions.a: The Comets.

questions.q: Why did Amara have to play in the goal?
questions.a: The usual goalie was sick.

questions.q: Amara put on goalie gloves that "felt strange and puffy." What does "puffy" mean?
questions.a: Soft and thick, puffed up.

questions.q: How did Amara feel when Coach Ben first asked her to play goalie?
questions.a: Nervous (worried or scared).

questions.q: Why did the author include what Kai said to Amara?
questions.a: It shows how his advice helped her do better and catch the ball.

placement.title: Busy Honeybees
paragraphs: Honeybees live together in a home called a hive. A big hive can hold thousands of bees. Each hive has just one queen. Her job is to lay eggs. She lays lots of eggs each day. The other bees take care of her.

Most bees in a hive are worker bees. All the workers are female. They clean the hive. They feed the baby bees. They also fly out to find flowers. They drink a sweet juice from the flowers. It is called nectar. Back home, they turn the nectar into honey. The bees eat the honey in winter.

When a worker finds good flowers, she does a dance. She wiggles and turns in a special way. The dance tells the other bees where to go. Then they can fly right to the flowers. Bees also carry pollen from flower to flower. This helps new plants and fruits grow.

questions.q: How many queen bees does each hive have?
questions.a: One.

questions.q: What is the sweet juice that bees drink from flowers called?
questions.a: Nectar.

questions.q: The bees "carry pollen from flower to flower," and this "helps new plants and fruits grow." What is "pollen"?
questions.a: A powder in flowers that helps new plants grow.

questions.q: Why do bees need to store honey before winter?
questions.a: There are few or no flowers in winter, so they need saved food.

questions.q: Why did the author tell about the bee dance?
questions.a: To show how bees share where to find flowers.

placement.title: Our Moon
paragraphs: The moon is the brightest thing in our night sky. But the moon does not make its own light. Instead, sunlight shines on it. The light bounces off the moon and comes to us. That is why we can see it at night.

The moon goes around Earth. Each trip takes about one month. As it moves, it seems to change shape. Some nights it looks round and full. Other nights it is a thin curve. The moon is not really changing. We just see different parts of its sunny side.

The moon is covered in gray dust and rocks. It has many round holes called craters. Space rocks crashed into the moon and made them. There is no air or wind there. In 1969, people walked on the moon for the first time. Their footprints are still there today, because no wind can blow them away.

questions.q: How long does it take the moon to go around Earth?
questions.a: About one month.

questions.q: In what year did people first walk on the moon?
The moon has "round holes called craters" that space rocks made. What are "craters"?
questions.a: Round holes made when space rocks crashed into the moon.

questions.q: Why would footprints on Earth's beach not last as long as footprints on the moon?
questions.a: Wind (and water) on Earth would wipe them away; the moon has no wind.

questions.q: The first paragraph asks why we can see the moon. How does the author answer it?
questions.a: By explaining that sunlight bounces off the moon to us.

placement.title: Grandpa's Workbench
paragraphs: On Saturday, Omar went to his grandpa's garage. It smelled like sawdust and old paint. A stack of boards sat on the workbench. "Today we will build a birdhouse," Grandpa said with a wink. Omar had wanted to build one all winter.

First, they measured each board. Grandpa showed Omar how to draw a straight line. Then Grandpa cut the boards. Omar held them steady while he cut. Omar hammered the nails himself. A few nails bent, so he pulled them out and tried again. Grandpa said that all builders make mistakes. By lunch, the walls and roof were done.

After lunch, Omar painted the birdhouse bright blue. Grandpa drilled a round hole in the front for a door. They hung it on the maple tree by the kitchen window. Two weeks later, Omar saw a small brown bird. It was carrying twigs inside. He ran to tell Grandpa right away.

questions.q: What color did Omar paint the birdhouse?
questions.a: Bright blue.

questions.q: Where did they hang the birdhouse?
questions.a: On the maple tree by the kitchen window.

questions.q: Omar held the boards "steady" while Grandpa cut them. What does "steady" mean?
questions.a: Still, not moving or shaking.

questions.q: Why was the brown bird carrying twigs into the birdhouse?
questions.a: It was building a nest there.

questions.q: Why did the author include the part about the bent nails?
questions.a: To show that Omar made mistakes but kept trying, and that mistakes are okay.

placement.title: Penguin Dads
paragraphs: Emperor penguins are the biggest penguins in the world. They live in Antarctica. It is one of the coldest places on Earth. These birds cannot fly, but they swim very well. They dive deep into the icy sea to catch fish.

In winter, a mother penguin lays one egg. Then she passes it to the father. He holds it on top of his feet. A warm flap of skin covers the egg like a blanket. The mother walks back to the sea to eat. She may be gone for about two months. All that time, the father does not eat at all. He just keeps the egg warm.

To stay warm, the fathers stand close together in a big huddle. They take turns in the middle, where it is warmest. Around the time the chick hatches, the mother comes back. She brings food in her belly for the baby. Then the hungry father can finally go eat.

questions.q: Where do emperor penguins live?
questions.a: Antarctica.

questions.q: Where does the father penguin hold the egg?
questions.a: On top of his feet.

questions.q: The fathers "stand close together in a big huddle" to stay warm. What is a "huddle"?
questions.a: A tight group standing close together.

questions.q: Why does the father penguin get very hungry?
questions.a: He does not eat the whole time the mother is gone, about two months.

questions.q: How is the second paragraph organized?
questions.a: In time order: the egg is laid, passed to the father, and he waits while the mother eats.

placement.title: The Drum in the Hallway
paragraphs: Jayden wanted to play the drums more than anything. His aunt gave him an old drum set for his birthday. It sat in the hallway by his bedroom. Every day after school, he tapped out beats with his wooden sticks. The trouble was the noise. His baby sister napped every afternoon.

One day his sister woke up crying. Mom came out of her room looking tired. "Jayden, we need a better plan," she said gently. Jayden felt bad. He did not want to stop practicing. So he sat down and thought hard about it.

That evening, he had an idea. He asked Mr. Hill, his music teacher, for help. Mr. Hill gave him soft rubber pads to put on top of the drums. They made the drums much quieter. Jayden also started practicing before nap time instead of during it. A month later, he played a song at the school concert. His mom and sister clapped in the front row.

questions.q: Who gave Jayden the drum set?
questions.a: His aunt.

questions.q: What did Mr. Hill give Jayden?
questions.a: Soft rubber pads to put on the drums.

questions.q: Mom said "we need a better plan" after the noise woke the baby. Jayden "did not want to stop practicing." What does "practicing" mean?
questions.a: Doing something again and again to get better at it.

questions.q: Why did the baby wake up crying?
questions.a: Jayden's loud drumming woke her up.

questions.q: The story is built around a problem. What was the problem, and what two things solved it?
questions.a: The drums woke the baby; rubber pads made them quieter, and he practiced before nap time.

placement.title: The Floating Island
paragraphs: Each Friday night, Zoe and her big brother Malik played a video game. In the game, you could build whole worlds out of blocks. This week they wanted to make a floating island high above the sea. Malik wanted a castle on it. Zoe wanted a giant garden.

At first they argued, and no one built a thing. Then Zoe had an idea. They could split the island in half. Malik would build his castle on one side. She would plant her garden on the other. They joined the two halves with a long rope bridge. Zoe made water pour off the edges into the sea.

By the end of the night, the island looked better than they had dreamed. Malik said the garden made his castle look even grander. Zoe said the tall towers looked great above her flowers. Before bed, they made a list of plans for next Friday. At the top, Malik wrote one word: together.

questions.q: What did Malik want to build on the island?
questions.a: A castle.

questions.q: What connected the two halves of the island?
questions.a: A long rope bridge.

questions.q: Malik said the garden made his castle look "even grander." What does "grander" mean?
questions.a: Bigger and more impressive or fancy.

questions.q: Why did Malik write the word "together" at the top of the list?
questions.a: He learned they built something better when they worked together.

questions.q: How does the passage show a change from the beginning to the end?
questions.a: It starts with them arguing and ends with them working as a team and happy.

placement.title: Mountains of Fire
paragraphs: Deep under the ground, it is so hot that rock can melt. This melted rock is called magma. Sometimes magma pushes up through cracks in the ground. When it reaches the top, a volcano can erupt. Once the hot rock comes out, it gets a new name. Now it is called lava.

Lava can be much hotter than an oven. It glows bright orange and red as it flows. Some volcanoes ooze lava slowly, like thick syrup. Others blast clouds of ash high into the sky. When lava cools, it turns hard. It becomes new rock. Over many years, layer after layer of rock can build a tall mountain.

Volcanoes can even make new land. The islands of Hawaii were built by volcanoes that rose up from the sea floor. Some scientists spend their lives studying volcanoes. They use special tools to check the ground and the gas near a volcano. Their work helps them warn people when one may blow soon.

questions.q: What is melted rock called while it is still under the ground?
questions.a: Magma.

questions.q: What islands were formed by volcanoes rising from the ocean floor?
questions.a: The islands of Hawaii.

questions.q: Some volcanoes "ooze lava slowly, like thick syrup." What does "ooze" mean?
questions.a: To flow out slowly.

questions.q: Why is the work of scientists who study volcanoes important to people who live near them?
questions.a: Their warnings give people time to get to safety before an eruption.

questions.q: Why does the author compare lava to an oven and to syrup?
questions.a: To help readers picture how hot lava is and how slowly some of it moves.

placement.title: A Day at the Fire Station
paragraphs: Firefighters do much more than put out fires. They work at a fire station. They often stay there for a full day and night. The station has a kitchen, beds, and a big garage for the trucks. When an alarm rings, the crew must be ready to go in a minute or two.

Their gear is heavy. Each one wears a thick coat, boots, a helmet, and a tank of air on the back. The air tank lets them breathe inside smoky buildings. Fire trucks carry long hoses, tall ladders, and lots of tools. The crew practices using this equipment again and again. Practice helps them work fast and stay safe.

Firefighters also help people who are sick or hurt. Many of them are trained to give first aid. They visit schools to teach kids how to stay safe from fire too. They tell families to test their smoke alarms often. They teach kids to stay low under smoke. They also say to pick a meeting place outside the home.

questions.q: What does the air tank let firefighters do?
questions.a: Breathe inside smoky buildings.

questions.q: What do firefighters remind families to test?
questions.a: Their smoke alarms.

questions.q: Fire trucks carry "long hoses, tall ladders, and lots of tools," and the crew practices "using this equipment." What does "equipment" mean?
questions.a: The tools and gear needed to do a job.

questions.q: Why does a fire station have a kitchen and beds?
questions.a: Firefighters stay there a full day and night, so they need to eat and sleep there.

questions.q: The first sentence says firefighters do more than put out fires. How does the rest of the passage support this?
questions.a: It tells other jobs they do, like first aid and teaching kids how to stay safe from fire.

placement.title: Pancakes for Mom
paragraphs: Rosa woke up early on Sunday because it was her mom's birthday. She and her dad had planned a secret breakfast all week. While Mom slept, they tiptoed into the kitchen. They pulled out flour, eggs, milk, and a bowl of fresh blueberries.

Dad read the recipe out loud while Rosa measured each ingredient with care. She cracked two eggs, and a tiny piece of shell fell into the bowl. She scooped it out with a spoon and kept going. When the batter was ready, Dad heated the pan. Rosa dropped blueberries into each pancake as it cooked. The first one burned on one side, but the rest came out golden and fluffy.

Rosa put the best pancakes on a plate and stuck a candle on top. She carried the plate up the stairs very slowly. Then she and Dad sang loudly as they opened the bedroom door. Mom sat up and laughed. She said it was the best birthday breakfast she had ever eaten.

questions.q: Why did Rosa wake up early on Sunday?
questions.a: It was her mom's birthday.

questions.q: What fruit did Rosa put in the pancakes?
questions.a: Blueberries.

questions.q: Rosa "measured each ingredient with care" before mixing the flour, eggs, and milk. What is an "ingredient"?
questions.a: One of the foods that go into a recipe.

questions.q: Why did Rosa and her dad tiptoe into the kitchen?
questions.a: They wanted to keep the breakfast a surprise and not wake Mom.

questions.q: Why did the author include the burned pancake and the piece of shell?
questions.a: To show small problems Rosa fixed or worked through while cooking.

placement.title: The Amazing Octopus
paragraphs: An octopus is a sea animal with eight long arms and a soft, round body. It has no bones at all. Because of this, it can squeeze its body through tiny cracks between rocks. A large octopus can slip through a hole about the size of a coin.

Each arm is lined with rows of suction cups. These cups help the octopus grab and hold onto things. They can also taste whatever they touch! An octopus has three hearts and blue blood. It is also one of the smartest animals in the ocean. Scientists have watched octopuses open jars and solve simple puzzles.

The octopus has clever ways to stay safe. It can change the color of its skin in less than a second. This lets it blend in with sand, rocks, or coral. If a hungry fish still spots it, the octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink. While the fish is confused, the octopus zooms away.

questions.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.a: Three.

questions.q: What can an octopus squirt when a hungry fish spots it?
questions.a: A cloud of dark ink.

questions.q: An octopus can change color so it can "blend in with sand, rocks, or coral." What does "blend in" mean?
questions.a: To look like the things around it so it is hard to see.

questions.q: How does the dark ink help the octopus get away?
questions.a: It hides the octopus or confuses the fish so the octopus can escape.

questions.q: How is the passage organized?
questions.a: By topic: its body and no bones, then its arms and brain, then how it stays safe.

placement.title: The Backyard Weather Station
paragraphs: For the science fair, Eli built a weather station in his backyard. He cut a plastic bottle to make a rain gauge and marked lines on the side with a ruler. He also made a wind vane from a straw, a pencil, and a paper arrow.

Each morning before school, Eli checked his station and wrote the numbers in a notebook. He wrote down the temperature, how much rain fell, and which way the wind blew. On Tuesday, the arrow pointed west, and dark clouds were rolling in. Eli predicted that it would rain by the afternoon. He was right. By dinnertime, the bottle held almost an inch of water.

After two weeks, Eli turned his notes into a bright chart. He noticed that rainy days often came after the wind changed. At the fair, his teacher looked at the chart closely. She said he was thinking just like a real weather scientist. Eli grinned and decided to keep his station going all year.

questions.q: What did Eli use to make his rain gauge?
questions.a: A plastic bottle.

questions.q: How much rain was in the bottle by dinnertime on Tuesday?
questions.a: Almost an inch.

questions.q: Eli "predicted that it would rain by the afternoon," and he was right. What does "predicted" mean?
questions.a: Said what would happen before it happened.

questions.q: What clues did Eli use to guess it would rain on Tuesday?
questions.a: The wind arrow pointed west and dark clouds were rolling in.

questions.q: Why did the author include the part about the dark clouds on Tuesday?
questions.a: To give an example of Eli using his station to make a correct prediction.

placement.title: The Tryout
paragraphs: Imani and her best friend Sofia had practiced basketball together every afternoon all summer long. They both hoped to make the school team, but only a few spots were open. On the morning of tryouts, Imani's hands felt so shaky that she could barely tie her shoes.

The coach started with dribbling drills, and Imani lost the ball twice in a row. She wanted to give up and walk off the court. Then Sofia caught her eye and tapped two fingers on her own chest. It was their secret signal, and it meant, "Breathe and remember our practice." Imani let her shoulders drop, and her next shots swished right through the net.

A week later, the coach posted the team list on the gym door. Imani's name was on it, but Sofia's was not. Imani did not know if she should cheer or hug her friend. Sofia smiled and said she would keep practicing and try again next year. Then she asked Imani to help her get ready.

questions.q: How long had Imani and Sofia practiced together?
questions.a: Every afternoon, all summer long.

questions.q: Where did the coach post the team list?
questions.a: On the gym door.

questions.q: Imani's "hands felt so shaky that she could barely tie her shoes." What does "barely" mean?
questions.a: Only just, almost not.

questions.q: Why did Imani not know if she should cheer or hug Sofia?
questions.a: She was happy she made the team but sad that Sofia did not.

questions.q: Why did the author include the secret signal?
questions.a: It shows how Sofia helped Imani calm down and do well, even while trying out herself.

placement.title: Stegosaurus
paragraphs: Stegosaurus was a large dinosaur that ate plants and lived about 150 million years ago. Most of its fossils have been found in the western United States. It was about as long as a school bus, but it moved slowly on four thick legs. Its back legs were longer than its front legs, so its head stayed low.

The best-known part of Stegosaurus was the row of big, bony plates along its back. Scientists are not sure what the plates were for. Some think they helped the dinosaur warm up or cool down. Others think the plates helped other dinosaurs recognize it, the way bright feathers help birds tell each other apart.

At the end of its tail were four sharp spikes. It could swing its tail to keep hungry meat-eaters away. This huge animal also had a very small brain for its size. We know all of this from fossil bones. No person ever saw a living Stegosaurus.

questions.q: About how long ago did Stegosaurus live?
questions.a: About 150 million years ago.

questions.q: How many spikes were at the end of its tail?
questions.a: Four.

questions.q: The plates may have helped other dinosaurs "recognize" it, "the way bright feathers help birds tell each other apart." What does "recognize" mean?
questions.a: To know who or what something is by seeing it.

questions.q: Why do scientists have different ideas about what the plates were for?
questions.a: No one ever saw a living Stegosaurus, so they can only guess from fossils.

questions.q: What does each paragraph mainly tell about?
questions.a: 1: when it lived and its size; 2: its back plates; 3: its tail spikes, small brain, and how we know these facts.

placement.title: How a Rainbow Forms
paragraphs: Sunlight looks white or yellow to us, but it is really a mix of many colors. Most of the time these colors travel as a group, so we cannot see them separately. A rainbow forms when the colors in sunlight get split apart.

Raindrops are what do the job. When sunlight goes into a drop of water, the light bends. Each color bends by a slightly changed amount, so the colors spread out. The light then bounces off the back of the drop and comes out again. Millions of drops in the air work as a team. The result is a huge curved band of color across the sky.

The colors of a rainbow always come in the same order. Red is on the outside of the curve, and violet is on the inside. To see a rainbow, you must stand with the sun at your back and rain in front of you. That is why rainbows often show up late in the day, just after a summer shower.

questions.q: What does sunlight go into to make a rainbow?
questions.a: Raindrops (drops of water).

questions.q: Which color is on the outside of a rainbow's curve?
questions.a: Red.

questions.q: Most of the time the colors travel as a group, "so we cannot see them separately." What does "separately" mean?
questions.a: Apart from each other, one at a time.

questions.q: Why would you probably not see a rainbow on a sunny day with no rain or clouds at all?
questions.a: There is no rain in the air to split the sunlight.

questions.q: Why does the author explain that sunlight is a mix of colors before talking about raindrops?
questions.a: Readers need to know that first to understand how raindrops split light into a rainbow.

placement.title: The Sock-Sorting Machine
paragraphs: Theo had a problem that no one else in his family cared about. Each week, the laundry basket filled up with mismatched socks, and sorting them took him nearly an hour. For the school invention fair, he decided to build a machine to fix it for good.

His first design used a cardboard ramp and a set of boxes, but the socks kept getting tangled. Theo drew a new plan and added a small fan to pull the socks apart as they slid down. That one blew socks all over his bedroom floor, so his older cousin Hana told him to sort by color first instead of by size. So Theo glued a colored card above each box and adjusted the ramp.

After six attempts, the machine sorted most socks the right way in under ten minutes. At the fair, Theo explained each failed design and the last one. The judges said his notebook showed what true inventors do. He did not win first place, but he went home proud.

questions.q: How long did sorting socks take Theo before he built the machine?
questions.a: Nearly an hour.

questions.q: What did Theo add to his second plan to pull the socks apart?
questions.a: A small fan.

questions.q: Theo's socks were "mismatched," so sorting them took nearly an hour. What does "mismatched" mean?
questions.a: Not in matching pairs; mixed up.

questions.q: Why did the judges praise Theo's notebook?
questions.a: It showed he kept trying and learned from each failed design, like real inventors.

questions.q: Why does the author describe the failed designs in the middle paragraph?
questions.a: To show that inventing takes many tries and that Theo kept improving his idea.

placement.title: Perseverance on Mars
paragraphs: In February 2021, a robot about the size of a small car landed safely on Mars. Its name was Perseverance. It had flown through space for nearly seven months to get there. Scientists picked a landing spot in a wide crater that they think held a lake billions of years ago.

The rover carries cameras, rock tools, and even a way to hear sounds. Its main job is to look for signs that tiny living things may have lived on Mars long ago. It drills into rocks and seals small bits of them inside metal tubes. Scientists hope that a future trip will bring some of those tubes back to Earth so they can look at them up close.

The rover did not make the trip alone. Tucked under its belly was a small helicopter named Ingenuity. In April 2021, it became the first aircraft to make a powered flight on another planet. It was meant to fly only a handful of times, but it kept flying for almost three years.

questions.q: When did Perseverance land on Mars?
questions.a: February 2021.

questions.q: What was the name of the small helicopter?
questions.a: Ingenuity.

questions.q: Ingenuity "was meant to fly only a handful of times, but it kept flying for almost three years." What does "a handful" mean here?
questions.a: A small number, just a few.

questions.q: Why did scientists pick a landing spot that may once have held a lake?
questions.a: Living things need water, so an old lake is a good place to look for signs of past life.

questions.q: How is the third paragraph different from the first two?
questions.a: It moves from the rover to the helicopter it carried, Ingenuity.

placement.title: The Empty Lot
paragraphs: For years, the empty lot at the end of Maple Street held nothing but weeds, broken bricks, and dry dirt. Lila walked past it every day on her way to school and pictured it full of tomatoes and sunflowers. One spring, she finally asked her neighbors if they would help turn it into a garden.

At first, only Mrs. Ortiz from next door and an old builder named Mr. Green said yes. They cleared away the bricks and built four wooden beds for planting. Other neighbors saw the work and started to join in, bringing shovels, seeds, and buckets of rich soil. A hardware store gave them a long hose.

By late summer, the lot had been completely transformed. Rows of beans climbed tall poles, and sunflowers stood higher than the fence. Neighbors who had never spoken before now traded recipes and shared what they grew. On the last Saturday in August, they all had a picnic in the garden that Lila had once only pictured.

questions.q: What did the empty lot hold before the garden?
questions.a: Weeds, broken bricks, and dry dirt.

questions.q: What did the hardware store give them?
questions.a: A long hose.

questions.q: By late summer, "the lot had been completely transformed" with beans and sunflowers. What does "transformed" mean?
questions.a: Changed completely.

questions.q: How did the garden change the neighborhood besides growing food?
questions.a: It brought neighbors together; people who never talked became friends.

questions.q: Why does the author begin with the lot full of weeds and end with a picnic in the garden?
questions.a: To show how much the lot changed from the beginning to the end.

placement.title: The Missing Note
paragraphs: Kai had been practicing the same violin piece for three weeks, yet one hard part still sounded wrong every time. His finger had to slide quickly up the neck of the violin, and it always landed slightly too low. With the spring recital only five days away, he wondered if he should pick an easier song.

At his next lesson, Ms. Patel listened closely and asked him to play that part at half speed. Kai thought this was a ridiculous idea, since he wanted to play faster, not slower, but when he slowed down, he could hear exactly where his finger missed the note. Ms. Patel said musicians often practice slowly first so their hands memorize the correct movements.

All week, Kai played the part slowly and then gradually increased his speed each day. On the night of the recital, he walked onstage with his heart pounding. When he reached the hard part, his finger landed precisely on the note, and he smiled through the rest of the song.

questions.q: How many days away was the recital when the story began?
questions.a: Five days.

questions.q: At what speed did Ms. Patel ask Kai to play the hard part?
questions.a: Half speed.

questions.q: On the night of the recital, "his finger landed precisely on the note." What does "precisely" mean?
questions.a: Exactly; just right.

questions.q: Why did Kai smile through the rest of the song?
questions.a: He finally played the hard part right, so he felt proud and relieved.

questions.q: Why does the author tell us that Kai thought slow practice was a ridiculous idea?
questions.a: To show he doubted the advice at first, which makes it stronger when it works.

placement.title: Cities Under the Sea
paragraphs: Coral reefs may look like rocks, but corals are really tiny living things. Each coral is made of many small creatures called polyps. Over time, the polyps build hard shells from things in seawater, and those shells slowly pile up into huge reefs. The largest reef system in the world, the Great Barrier Reef, stretches more than a thousand miles along the coast of Australia.

Inside most corals that build reefs live tiny plant-like things called algae. The algae use sunlight to make food, and share much of it with the coral. In return, the coral gives the algae a safe place to live. When the ocean gets too warm, corals push the algae out and turn white, which scientists call bleaching.

Reefs cover a small part of the ocean floor, but they are home to a huge variety of life. Fish, sea turtles, crabs, and sea stars all need reefs for food and shelter. That is why people often call coral reefs the busy cities of the sea.

questions.q: What are the small creatures that make up a coral called?
questions.a: Polyps.

questions.q: Along what country's coast is the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.a: Australia.

questions.q: Fish, sea turtles, crabs, and sea stars all live on reefs, so reefs are home to "a huge variety of life." What does "variety" mean?
questions.a: Many different kinds.

questions.q: Why might a bleached coral have trouble staying healthy?
questions.a: It has lost the algae that gave it much of its food.

questions.q: Why does the author compare coral reefs to cities?
questions.a: Because, like cities, reefs are crowded with many kinds of living things that live and find food there.

placement.title: The Long Flight of the Monarch
paragraphs: Each fall, millions of monarchs in the eastern part of North America begin a long trip. They fly south to the high mountain forests of Mexico, and some travel close to three thousand miles. When they get there, they gather in such huge groups that the fir trees look as if they are covered in orange leaves.

What makes this trip even more remarkable is that no single monarch makes the whole round trip. Most of them live for only a few weeks in the summer. But the ones born at the end of summer are special, since they can live for up to eight months. These long-lived monarchs fly south and rest through the winter in the cool mountains.

In spring, they start flying north and lay eggs as they go. Their young keep going, one group after the next, until monarchs reach Canada again. On the way, the young eat just one kind of plant, called milkweed. Planting milkweed is one way people can help them.

questions.q: Where do eastern monarch butterflies fly each fall?
questions.a: To the mountain forests of Mexico.

questions.q: What is the only plant the young monarchs eat on the way?
questions.a: Milkweed.

questions.q: "No single monarch makes the whole round trip," and that makes the trip "even more remarkable." What does "remarkable" mean?
questions.a: Amazing; worth noticing or talking about.

questions.q: Why can a monarch born early in summer not make the trip to Mexico?
questions.a: It lives only a few weeks, too short for the long journey.

questions.q: Why does the author end with planting milkweed?
questions.a: To show readers one way they can help monarchs, since the young need milkweed to eat.
